questionCandidates.text: Now that you've reached the threshold of Ace Pilot, what part of the role do you want to make your own?

answers.text: I want to get on an opponent's tail and stay there, even when they try everything to shake me.
I want to be the hardest pilot to pin down in a dogfight, keeping my enemies guessing even while I stay in the fight.
I want to push a vehicle beyond ordinary speeds and still know exactly what I'm doing at the controls.
I want to keep a vehicle in one piece when a fight turns ugly, dodging the worst hits and holding together under fire.
I want to find attack angles nobody expects, slipping past a bigger opponent's guns to make my own strike count.
I want to know one kind of vehicle so thoroughly that piloting it becomes second nature.
I want to earn the kind of reputation that steadies the pilots flying beside me when the pressure is on.
I want to make every vehicle weapon shot count, whether the target is close enough to see clearly or barely in range.
I want to keep firing effectively in the middle of a dogfight, even when I'm working the guns instead of flying.
I want to disable an enemy vehicle by wrecking the systems it needs to keep fighting, not just hammer away at its hull.
I want to take the shot the moment an enemy gives me an opening, before it can get away.
I want to time my fire with another gunner so two well-placed hits land harder together.
I want to coax one decisive burst out of a vehicle weapon, even if that means giving it time to recover afterward.
I want to move and fight in zero gravity without feeling like I'm out of my element.
I want to be as capable in a ship's cramped corridors as I am at its controls when trouble comes aboard.
I want to stay on the move when a shipboard fight turns against me, slipping away before anyone can trap me.
I want to know how to raid a ship, disrupt its defenses, and get out before its crew can respond.
I want to call the right target and bring a whole squadron in on a coordinated attack run.
I want to keep the ships under my command in fighting shape when a battle starts going wrong.
I want to teach the flying and gunnery tricks I know so an entire squadron can benefit from them.
I want a squadron to maneuver as one unit, each pilot knowing how to use the opening the others create.
I want to guide a ship through an enemy blockade, making even heavy guns struggle to find a clean shot.
I want to turn speed into protection, making it harder for pursuers to hit my vehicle as I race away.
I want to fly so close to a larger vessel that its own bulk becomes cover for my escape.
I want to break through a dangerous approach without letting another pilot force me into a fight I never chose.
I want to fly close enough to another pilot that we can keep each other's vehicles in the fight.
I want to help the pilot beside me shake off an enemy before either of us gets trapped in a dogfight.
I want to use my own flying to turn aside a shot headed for a nearby ally.
I want to help a wingmate line up the shot that ends the fight, even if I don't get the credit.
I want anyone who fires on my wingmate to know I'll be answering with my own guns.
I don't want to be known for just one kind of craft. I want to grow comfortable flying anything from a speeder to a transport or starfighter.

scenes.title: The Closing Passage

mentor.speaker: Mayu
mentor.text: Tight passage, bad timing, two transports, and one very unfriendly patrol. Cute. Tell me what you do.

scenes.situation: You are piloting one of two transports carrying evacuees through shifting debris. The safe opening will close in moments. The other transport is losing speed, and a pursuing patrol craft is gaining. Both pilots can communicate, and your instruments can still read the debris. You have no authority over the other pilot.
scenes.question: You have moments to make a call. How do you handle it?

answers.text: I keep my transport moving through the opening. If I lose the escape for the people aboard, I have failed the responsibility already in my hands.
I move between the patrol and the damaged transport and try to spoil its line of fire. I want the other pilot to have a chance to get clear.
I call the other pilot and propose one timed path through the debris. We have a better chance if our maneuvers work together.
I read the debris and look for a second opening before I commit. A route neither of us noticed could save both transports.
I cut across the patrol's approach and try to draw it away from the damaged transport. If it takes the bait, I can bring it through a different gap.

scenes.title: The Disabled Target

mentor.speaker: Mayu
mentor.text: You have a target in sight. Congratulations. That was the easy part. Now tell me what that shot is actually for.

scenes.situation: During a relief-ship escort, you are temporarily operating a weapon station aboard an armed patrol craft while someone else pilots. A raider that fired on the convoy has lost much of its engine power, but its weapons are still active. A damaged freighter is nearby, and another friendly patrol craft is approaching. The raider may fire again before help arrives.
scenes.question: What do you do with the opportunity?

answers.text: I line up a careful shot at the raider's active weapons. I would rather remove its ability to threaten the convoy than simply tear the craft apart.
I fire as soon as I have a clear shot. Letting the raider keep its guns trained on the freighter is a risk I will not extend.
I contact the approaching patrol and coordinate one focused volley. Two attacks at the right moment may end the danger faster than scattered fire.
I tell our pilot to interpose the patrol craft between the raider and the freighter. Protecting the freighter matters more than taking the final shot.
I track the raider's weapon arcs and relay a clear threat report to the approaching patrol. I want them ready to act without guessing.

scenes.title: The Broken Formation

mentor.speaker: Mayu
mentor.text: Everyone looks brilliant in a perfect formation. Then the comms crackle and things get interesting. Your move, ace.

scenes.situation: You are one of several independent pilots helping escort survey craft through dangerous airspace. Interference disrupts their shared navigation channel, and the loose formation begins to scatter. One hostile fast craft slips toward an exposed flank. A short-range voice channel still works, but nobody has appointed you to command the group.
scenes.question: How do you respond to the break in coordination?

answers.text: I use the surviving channel to suggest a simple regrouping pattern. We can close the gaps if everyone understands the same plan.
I move to the exposed flank and hold a defensive line. If the intruder commits to an attack, I want it coming through me first.
I move to intercept the intruder before it reaches the survey craft. If it has to react to me, the others get time to regroup.
I match the course of one isolated escort and stay with it. Keeping two craft together is better than letting each be picked off alone.
I use the instruments we still have to call out the intruder's position and relay course changes. Everyone should be working from the same picture.

scenes.title: The Failing Systems

mentor.speaker: Mayu
mentor.text: Gravity's off, the hatch is jammed, the bridge is yelling, and a mystery ship wants to say hello. Nice little quiet trip. What do you do?

scenes.situation: You are aboard a transport that has lost power while crossing a dangerous stretch of space. Artificial gravity has failed, a security hatch has trapped passengers in an aft compartment, and the bridge reports unstable maneuvering controls. An unidentified craft is approaching the airlock without answering hails. Maintenance access and internal comms still work. Nobody has appointed you to command the response.
scenes.question: Where do you put your effort first?

answers.text: I make my way through the zero-gravity passage to help the bridge regain control. If the transport cannot maneuver, every other danger gets worse.
I open the maintenance access and work to restore essential power. That could free the hatch and give the bridge more control.
I head toward the trapped passengers and find a way to move them to a safer compartment. Getting people clear is the problem I can solve now.
I take a position near the airlock and watch the approaching craft. I do not know if it is hostile, but I will not leave that entrance unguarded.
I use the comms to suggest a split response: someone on power, someone helping passengers, and someone watching the airlock. We need all three covered.

scenes.title: The Impossible Route

mentor.speaker: Mayu
mentor.text: Short route, bad weather, ticking clock. Whoever planned this job clearly has a sense of humor. What's your play?

scenes.situation: An isolated medical station needs supplies before a storm front closes the landing zone. You are piloting the delivery vehicle. The marked route is safer but probably too slow; an unfamiliar canyon route is much shorter and has dangerous crosswinds. An old survey buoy offers incomplete weather readings. Another pilot in the area can answer your comms, and the station can coordinate a different handoff if asked.
scenes.question: How do you give the delivery its best chance?

answers.text: I take the canyon and rely on disciplined control to handle the crosswinds. The faster route is risky, but reaching the station in time matters.
I study the buoy's readings and chart the least dangerous line through the canyon. I want a shortcut I understand, not a blind leap.
I use the marked route and look for safe opportunities to increase my pace. A dependable delivery is better than wrecking the only supplies.
I contact the other pilot and ask for live crosswind reports as I approach. Sharing information may make the unfamiliar route manageable.
I ask the station to prepare a pickup point closer to the canyon mouth. Changing the handoff could solve a problem raw speed will not.

scenes.title: The Vanishing Trail

mentor.speaker: Kex Varon
mentor.text: A missing person, three false leads, and a clock. A trigger finger will not find the right door.

scenes.situation: A client wants a missing courier found alive. Records put the courier at a busy port, but the trail ends there. Witnesses disagree, surveillance is incomplete, and the client cannot explain why the courier vanished. You have no evidence that the courier is guilty or in immediate danger.
scenes.question: Where do you begin?

answers.text: I examine the last reliable sighting and rebuild the route from small physical details before I follow anyone's accusation.
I question the people who handled the courier's business, comparing their accounts until a contradiction gives me a solid lead.
I trace travel payments, terminal access, and communications to find a route the courier could not easily erase.
I inspect who gains from the disappearance before I commit to any one story. A false client is as dangerous as a false trail.
I watch the last known location discreetly and let anyone following the same trail expose themselves before I move.

scenes.title: The Live Handoff

mentor.speaker: Kex Varon
mentor.text: The contract says alive. That does not mean the quarry intends to cooperate.

scenes.situation: You have located a courier who is wanted for questioning under a valid contract specifying live delivery. The courier is in a crowded market and looks ready to flee. Armed security personnel are nearby, but they are not working for you. A violent confrontation could injure bystanders or make a lawful handoff impossible.
scenes.question: How do you attempt the capture?

answers.text: I approach openly, identify the contract, and offer the courier a chance to come peacefully before anyone reaches for a weapon.
I take a position that cuts off the clearest exit, keeping the crowd out of the line of any confrontation.
I look for a safe moment to seize and restrain the courier without drawing a crowd into the struggle.
I coordinate a lawful handoff with local security so the courier has less reason to panic or fight.
I let the courier move and follow from a distance until there is a safer place to make the attempt.

scenes.title: The Price of the Contract

mentor.speaker: Kex Varon
mentor.text: The target was the easy part. The payment conversation is where mistakes become expensive.

scenes.situation: You reach a meeting with a prospective employer who wants a fugitive located. The employer offers a high fee but refuses to disclose why the fugitive is wanted. A separate witness claims the employer has concealed important facts. The employer demands a decision before another hunter takes the offer.
scenes.question: What terms do you set?

answers.text: I refuse to accept a target on the employer's word alone. I verify the contract and the fugitive's status before I agree.
I negotiate for clear conditions, a fair fee, and payment terms that do not leave me carrying all the risk.
I make it clear that my reputation has a price. If the employer wants my services, they answer my questions first.
I speak to the witness privately and test both accounts. I want enough information to make my own decision.
I decline this offer and take a lower-paying assignment whose objective and limits I can actually judge.

scenes.title: The Quarry Who Feels You Coming

mentor.speaker: Kex Varon
mentor.text: Some targets see the net before it closes. Then you check the net twice.

scenes.situation: A credible lead suggests a missing suspect can sense danger through the Force. You are not certain what the suspect can do. You have a public sighting, a possible safe house, and a witness who will only talk at dusk. The contract permits capture, but you must first decide how to approach someone who may anticipate you.
scenes.question: How do you adjust your plan?

answers.text: I keep my approach ordinary and quiet, using observation and cover instead of betting on tricks I do not possess.
I study the suspect's known habits and prepare fallback positions so one sensed approach does not end the hunt.
I choose a position with a clear retreat and keep my distance until I understand what the suspect can do.
I speak with the witness and look for a way to earn the suspect's cooperation before forcing an encounter.
I consider the rites of a tradition I have actually trained in, if that path is open to me; otherwise I rely on what I can verify.

scenes.title: The Hunter Becomes the Mark

mentor.speaker: Kex Varon
mentor.text: You have the lead. Then the lead turns around and looks right at you. That is the part worth planning for.

scenes.situation: You locate a dangerous fugitive at an abandoned loading yard. The fugitive has taken cover near several unoccupied cargo containers and seems to be waiting. The exits are visible but there may be accomplices nearby. You can communicate with one independent contact who is a few blocks away.
scenes.question: What is your next move?

answers.text: I hold my distance and watch for movement until I know whether the fugitive is alone or trying to draw me in.
I prepare one deliberate shot against the threat that matters most, rather than firing at every movement.
I move between covered positions, looking for an angle that denies the fugitive an easy escape.
I call my contact, share what I can confirm, and ask them to watch the far exit rather than charge in.
I signal the fugitive that I know this may be a trap and offer a chance to stand down before I close.

scenes.title: The Deal With Two Prices

mentor.speaker: Tío the Hutt
mentor.text: Ah, two offers and neither is the whole truth. Business is improving already.

scenes.situation: Two freight operators want your help negotiating access to a disputed warehouse. Both promise future favors, but each is withholding something about the lease. The warehouse also supplies a neighborhood clinic. You have influence with neither party yet, and neither is obligated to follow your advice.
scenes.question: How would you try to shape the deal?

answers.text: I ask what each operator really needs, then offer an exchange that gives both a reason to honor the agreement.
I establish which legal claim is strongest and make access contingent on a transparent record of obligations.
I let each party see that a dishonest deal will cost them access to my help and to each other.
I bring the clinic into the negotiation so its needs become the condition both operators must account for.
I decline to settle a deal built on missing facts and quietly investigate why both sides want the warehouse.

scenes.title: The Broken Network

mentor.speaker: Tío the Hutt
mentor.text: You want people to depend on your word? Start by learning what happens when one of them stops answering.

scenes.situation: A small coalition of traders and neighborhood organizers has asked you to advise its delivery network. One courier has disappeared, another threatens to quit, and a local rival is offering easier terms to defectors. You do not own this network or command the people in it. Without a plan, deliveries may stop.
scenes.question: What do you advise first?

answers.text: I meet the couriers individually, find out why trust has failed, and offer a reason to stay that goes beyond threats.
I divide critical deliveries among independent routes so one missing courier cannot collapse everything.
I propose recruiting a specialist who understands the rival's methods before we expand the network.
I speak with the rival directly and see whether a limited partnership serves both sides better than a prolonged contest.
I secure the most vulnerable delivery first and let the coalition judge the results before asking for more responsibility.

scenes.title: The Public Challenge

mentor.speaker: Tío the Hutt
mentor.text: One loud rival and an audience. Careful. The audience is the part you keep afterward.

scenes.situation: At a public meeting, a rival broker accuses you of cheating a mutual client and demands that you surrender an agreed payment. The broker has several supporters, but nobody is yet violent. Some witnesses doubt the accusation; others are waiting to see whether you escalate.
scenes.question: How do you respond?

answers.text: I want the Force powers I use to strike with greater force when a single blow must matter.
I want to reach beyond the usual limits of my powers without surrendering the ability to see what I affect.
I want a power meant for one person to reach others when I need to protect or confront more than one.
I want to call on a Force power in the smallest opening, before the moment passes.
I want to shape a sweeping Force power so it reaches where it is needed and spares those I choose.
I want to hold a Force power through the hardest moments without giving all my attention to maintaining it.
I want to set one Force power in motion and have another follow at the right moment, like two currents meeting.
I want to call on powers that protect me even when injuries and exhaustion cloud my concentration.
I want to make the dark side itself sharpen the effect of my powers against those less steeped in it than I am.
I want my damaging Force powers to weaken a foe’s ability to carry on, not merely wound them.
I want to expand the reach of my area powers when an entire battlefield needs to feel their effect.
I want the light side to give my powers an edge against those who have embraced the dark.
I want my powers to begin somewhere other than where I stand, changing where an enemy expects danger or help to come from.
I want to learn from the Force knowledge carried by others and preserve what I discover for those who follow.
I want to share a power I know with an apprentice who has learned enough to carry that knowledge onward.

scenes.title: The Forking Vision

mentor.speaker: Riquis
mentor.text: A dream points to two roads. Beware the certainty that makes one of them real.

scenes.situation: An elder brings you an account of a troubling vision: a flood will threaten a settlement, but the vision places the danger in two different valleys at once. The weather is changing, and moving everyone without evidence could create a different danger. You have heard the account; you have not necessarily received a vision yourself.
scenes.question: How do you decide where to act?

answers.text: I compare the elder's account with weather, terrain, and the settlements' immediate vulnerabilities before treating either valley as certain.
I would seek guidance through the Force if I have a legitimate way to do so, while remembering that a vision can be incomplete.
I warn both settlements of plausible danger and help them prepare without declaring either future inevitable.
I visit the terrain most likely to hide the flood's cause and look for physical signs that would distinguish the two warnings.
I ask the elder how the warning came and what might have been misunderstood before I change anyone's fate.

scenes.title: The Shifting Current

mentor.speaker: Riquis
mentor.text: The current is strong enough to drown the shoreline. The question is where you let it flow.

scenes.situation: A dangerous energy disturbance is spreading through an abandoned industrial platform. An automated defense system fires at anyone approaching the shutdown controls. A rescue team is nearby but not in the direct line of fire. You may have Force powers, conventional tools, or neither of the specialized secrets suggested by this problem; only actual owned abilities can be used.
scenes.question: What would be your preferred way to resolve the threat?

answers.text: I aim to affect the defense system precisely and spare the rescue team, even if that means using a smaller effect.
I would extend the reach of a power I actually possess so I could reach the shutdown point without bringing others into danger.
I would use one rapid, decisive effort when the defenses expose a safe opening, rather than letting the threat grow.
I would coordinate several carefully placed effects to protect the rescue team's approach, choosing restraint over the broadest blast.
I would first search for a conventional shutdown or a way to reduce the disturbance before spending a scarce Force resource.

scenes.title: The Burden of the Vessel

mentor.speaker: Riquis
mentor.text: The body is a vessel. So is a promise. Which one will you ask to carry the weight?

scenes.situation: A small group has escaped a hazardous area. One person is injured, another is exhausted, and an unstable barrier still threatens the group's shelter. Supplies are scarce, and everyone has a different idea of which danger comes first. You know only what the current character sheet confirms about your Force and medical capabilities.
scenes.question: Where do you place your effort?

answers.text: I care for the injured person first, using treatment methods and any Force healing I have actually learned.
I work to strengthen the shelter's defense so no one is injured again while help is arranged.
I direct the group to conserve supplies and rotate the exhausted person out of danger while we make a plan.
I look for a way to recover a spent Force power within my actual limits before using another effect.
I would use a rare, demanding Force technique to steady those around me only if I had learned it and could meet its price.

scenes.title: The Voice Behind the Thought

mentor.speaker: Riquis
mentor.text: An unwanted voice arrives inside a thought. The first question is whether you must answer it at all.

scenes.situation: Several travelers report that an unseen presence has tried to influence their decisions near an abandoned shrine. One traveler has begun repeating a stranger's instructions. Others are frightened, but nobody can identify the source. You can reach the shrine on foot, or keep the group safely away while investigating.
scenes.question: How do you respond?

answers.text: I move the travelers away from the shrine and help them make choices without the unseen voice pressing on them.
I investigate the source carefully, looking for evidence of a device, trick or Force effect before confronting it.
I would use an honest, voluntary mental link with a willing traveler if I knew how, to understand what they are experiencing.
I would confront the influence directly, relying on the mental defenses I actually possess rather than treating every thought as an order.
I would challenge the false instructions aloud so the travelers can test them against what they know.

scenes.title: The Unfinished Teaching

mentor.speaker: Riquis
mentor.text: A secret is a seed. Plant it carelessly, and you may never know what grows.

scenes.situation: A keeper of an old sanctuary offers to show you a damaged archive containing Force teachings from several traditions. The keeper asks whether the archive should be restored, shared with students, or sealed until its origin is understood. Some passages appear to require initiation into traditions you have not established any connection with.
scenes.question: What responsibility would you accept?

answers.text: I preserve the archive as faithfully as I can and document what is known before anyone changes the texts.
I compare the teachings with what I have truly learned, separating common principles from practices reserved for their own traditions.
I would teach a willing student only what I can responsibly explain and demonstrate, leaving the rest for further study.
I seek the keeper's consent to share carefully selected portions with other qualified seekers, so important knowledge is not lost.
I leave the most uncertain teachings sealed for now and go find someone with firsthand knowledge of their tradition.

introCandidates.label: Preferred introduction — DRAFT
introCandidates.text: Well, look who's earned a place among the quick draws. Nice. A pistol in the right hands can end a fight, save a life, or make one spectacular entrance. Me? I like having options. So tell me—what kind of Gunslinger are you going to be?

introCandidates.label: Alternative A — shorter
introCandidates.text: Look at you. Fast hands, a sharp eye, and room to become dangerous. There's more to this than drawing first, you know. What's your kind of gunfight?

introCandidates.label: Alternative B — more playful
introCandidates.text: So, you've reached the part where style starts counting as a survival skill. Try not to smile too much. Tell me what you're after: the perfect shot, the faster draw, or something cleverer?

questionCandidates.label: Question
questionCandidates.text: As a Gunslinger, what part of the craft do you want to make your own?

answers.text: I want to pick up the tiny details that tell me when somebody is about to make a move.
I want to stay on someone’s trail without slowing down every time the tracks get difficult.
I want my reflexes sharp enough that I can take the initiative before a fight gets away from me.
I want to regain the advantage later in a fight when everyone thinks the order of battle is settled.
I want to place a clean shot even when smoke or poor visibility obscures my target.
I want someone who catches me off guard to discover that I can still react to the attack.
I want to fight without being easily trapped between enemies on either side of me.
I want to spot the one weakness in an opponent’s defenses that lets my shot get past their damage reduction.
I want a little luck on my side when the odds are bad and I need one more chance to get through.
I want a perfect hit to give me the opening for another decisive action before the moment ends.
I want to try my hand at the gambling table and know when the odds are worth taking.
I want to turn a failed attempt into a second chance when my usual skill lets me down.
I want my luck to rescue a shot that would otherwise have missed its mark.
I want to turn a dangerous situation around with a shot nobody expected me to make.
I want a lucky bounce or unlikely angle to help me reach a target that thought it was safe.
I want to have a last chance to survive when a hit should have put me down.

I want to avert one disaster at the critical moment, even when I cannot explain how I managed it.
I want to make something useful of a moment when I seem to have no real training to fall back on.
I want to remain unpredictable enough that enemies cannot easily anticipate how I will respond.
I want to squeeze a better outcome out of a terrible shot when ordinary tactics are not enough.
I want a carefully aimed pistol shot to put a dangerous opponent on the defensive even if it does not drop them.
I want to keep an injured target from recovering quickly after I have knocked them off their stride.
I want my best shot to slow a target down and make it harder for them to escape.
I want to draw so quickly that even an ambush leaves me a chance to fire back.
I want to drop an enemy to the ground with a well-placed shot instead of relying on raw damage.
I want an opponent to misjudge me long enough that I can shoot while their guard is down.
I want my pistol training to keep several quick shots accurate instead of letting recoil and rushed timing ruin them.
I want to shoot a weapon out of someone’s hand without letting them close the distance on me.
I want a well-placed disarming shot to hurt a dangerous opponent as well as leave them weaponless.
I want to fire a powerful rapid shot without sacrificing the accuracy I have trained to maintain.
I want formal pistol dueling techniques that let me choose whether to aim, defend, or end the contest in one exchange.
I want to move and fight with a pistol without getting locked in place every time I pull the trigger.
I want to make an enemy feel surrounded even when I am covering them with my pistol from a distance.
I want to make a shot through darkness or heavy concealment when other shooters would lose the target.

I want to squeeze one extraordinarily fast shot into a moment when anyone else would be too slow.

scenes.title: A Draw Nobody Wants

mentor.speaker: Rajma
mentor.text: There's the stare. There's the silence. And there's the fool who thinks you have to draw first.

scenes.situation: A dispute in a crowded docking concourse turns into a standoff. An armed challenger fingers their holster while bystanders crowd the exits. You can see their hands but cannot know whether they intend to fire. The crowd has no cover and no one has drawn yet.
scenes.question: What do you do before the first shot?

answers.text: I watch their hands and weight shift, ready to react only when the threat becomes real.
I draw to a controlled position and make it clear that they can leave without a firefight.
I angle toward the crowd so my body and line of fire keep civilians out of the exchange.
I break the rhythm with a remark and force the challenger to reconsider before either of us fires.
I move toward cover and refuse to give anyone a clean opening while the threat is uncertain.

scenes.title: The Weapon in the Crowd

mentor.speaker: Rajma
mentor.text: One shot can solve a problem. Or make a hundred new ones. Try this one.

scenes.situation: In a marketplace, a frightened thief draws a blaster while holding a stolen case. Their finger is on the trigger, but several shoppers stand behind them. A security officer is approaching from the wrong angle. The thief has not fired.
scenes.question: How do you end the threat?

answers.text: I take the narrow opening to shoot the blaster from their hand before anyone is hurt.
I keep my weapon steady and order the officer to change position before anyone creates a crossfire.
I find a clear line and aim to stop the thief from moving, not to maximize the harm I cause.
I close the distance behind a stall and try to talk them into setting the case and blaster down.
I draw their attention onto me and give the shoppers a chance to retreat from the firing lane.

scenes.title: Smoke over the Platform

mentor.speaker: Rajma
mentor.text: Hard to look stylish when you can't see your boots. That's when the real shooting starts.

scenes.situation: An attacker fires from somewhere across a smoke-filled loading platform. The shapes of crates and machinery are visible, but the shooter is not. An ally is pinned behind a loading arm. You have only scattered clues about the attacker’s position.
scenes.question: How do you respond?

answers.text: I study the muzzle flashes and sound before committing to a shot at the most likely location.
I shift along the crates until I have an angle that doesn't put my ally behind the target.
I use short, deliberate shots to keep the attacker occupied while my ally moves.
I look for a safe ricochet angle off the machinery rather than fire blindly into the smoke.
I stop firing, relocate quietly, and wait for the attacker to betray their position.

scenes.title: Crossing the Killing Floor

mentor.speaker: Rajma
mentor.text: You can stand still and be a lovely target. Or you can do something useful.

scenes.situation: Two exposed doors connect a workshop to an evacuation tunnel. Hostile fire crosses the open floor between them. A small group must pass through, and an unattended carbine and a spare pistol lie among the tools. Taking either weapon costs time.
scenes.question: How do you get everyone across?

answers.text: I sprint between hard points and fire only when movement gives me a clean, useful shot.
I take the carbine, set a stable firing lane, and cover each person as they cross.
I carry a pistol in each hand and try to keep the attackers occupied while I move with the group.
I direct one person to watch the exit while I time the others' movement between enemy volleys.
I draw the attackers toward one side, then retreat behind cover so the tunnel stays open.

scenes.title: The Last Charge

mentor.speaker: Rajma
mentor.text: Lucky shots exist. So do bad plans wearing a nice hat. Which is this going to be?

scenes.situation: An armored mercenary blocks the only passage to an emergency control panel. Your blaster holds enough power for one reliable shot; its reserve cell is damaged. Behind the mercenary, a heavy door will seal in moments. You do not know how well the armor will hold.
scenes.question: What's your last useful move?

answers.text: I take time for one careful shot at the clearest weakness I can identify.
I gamble on a fast shot to distract the mercenary, then rush the door before it seals.
I aim at the doorway mechanism instead of the mercenary, hoping to change the problem without winning a duel.
I hold the shot as a threat and demand room to reach the controls.
I abandon the shot and search for a second path or an emergency release before the door closes.

introCandidates.text: You have come far enough to stand at the threshold of Knighthood. The trust placed in a Jedi Knight is not a command to become only one thing. scenes.title: The Bridge under Fire

mentor.speaker: Miraj
mentor.text: A blade can stop an attack. Judgment must decide where the blade belongs.

scenes.situation: A damaged footbridge leads civilians away from a collapsing district. Armed raiders fire from the far approach while people are still crossing. A security team can defend one end but cannot cover the entire span. You have a lightsaber if your build actually provides one; otherwise assume a suitable available weapon without special properties.
scenes.question: How do you protect the crossing?

answers.text: I take the exposed position and turn aside attacks until the last civilian reaches safety.
I cross to confront the raiders directly so they cannot keep firing on the bridge.

scenes.title: The Blade at the Gate

mentor.speaker: Darth Malbada
mentor.text: A challenge at the threshold. How tiresome. At least it may teach you something useful.

scenes.situation: An armed rival blocks the only safe entrance to a sealed training compound and demands a duel before allowing passage. They are alert, but have not attacked. The rival wears protective gear and has an unknown fighting style. Bystanders are behind you, beyond the rival’s immediate reach.
scenes.question: How do you claim passage?

I force the duel forward with aggressive attacks before the rival settles into a rhythm.
I maintain a guarded position and let the rival expose an opening by attacking first.
I choose protection and steady movement over speed so I can withstand a failed exchange.
I refuse the duel’s terms and seek another way into the compound that does not expose my back to the rival.

scenes.title: The Cracked Oath

mentor.speaker: Darth Malbada
mentor.text: Promises make such beautiful chains. Tell me which link you would break.

scenes.situation: A group of mercenaries guarding a hidden cache has split over an agreement with a powerful patron. One faction will honor the contract, another wants to leave, and a third threatens violence if anyone withdraws. You have no verified authority over the group; they ask whether you can offer them a workable settlement.
scenes.question: What do you do?

answers.text: I identify what each faction wants and propose a bargain that makes cooperation more profitable than betrayal.
I expose the one faction’s bluff in front of the others so its threat loses credibility.
I offer the faction that wants to leave a safe exit in exchange for useful information.
I refuse to negotiate while weapons are raised and secure a defensible position before returning to terms.
I challenge the patron’s assumptions about loyalty and ask the mercenaries to decide who truly earns their service.

scenes.title: The Price of the Relic

mentor.speaker: Darth Malbada
mentor.text: Power that arrives without a price is usually a trap. Even I prefer to know where it closes.

scenes.situation: A sealed workshop contains a damaged Sith artifact and notes describing how it might be restored. The notes propose using rare materials and a dangerous ritual. A technician can stabilize its casing without using the Force, but claims the artifact may lose some of its unique properties. You have not performed this rite before in the scenario.

answers.text: I study the inscriptions and the two different restoration methods before committing a resource.
I ask the technician to preserve the casing first, keeping the artifact intact for later study.
I test a limited ritual on a harmless component to learn what energy the artifact will demand.
I accept the loss of some unique properties in exchange for a safer, usable artifact.
I seal the workshop and prevent anyone from activating the relic until its dangers are understood.

scenes.title: The Unseen Advance

mentor.speaker: Darth Malbada
mentor.text: An impressive march is also an impressive target. There are subtler ways to arrive.

scenes.situation: A small strike party wants to pass a defended observation post to recover data from a hidden relay. Some members favor an open assault; others can move quietly but have limited equipment. They have asked for your assessment, not sworn service. If the alarm sounds, reinforcements may arrive.

I divide the party into a diversion and a retrieval team, synchronizing their actions by a clear signal.
I move alone to disable the alarm first, reducing risk for the others.
I recommend a brief, overwhelming strike on the exposed sentry position before reinforcements respond.
I organize a withdrawal route and signal before approaching, so failure does not trap the team.

scenes.title: The Unbound Current

mentor.speaker: Darth Malbada
mentor.text: There. Power without a steady hand. Decide what you intend to do before it decides for you.

answers.text: I try to compel the courier to disclose what they know, accepting the risk that forceful pressure may close other paths.
I study the courier and their movements for clues about who entrusted them with the device.
I offer safe passage for those the courier fears for, in exchange for a verifiable account of the device.
I trace the courier's contacts and travel records without relying on what they choose to tell me.
I organize immediate precautions for the settlement while others investigate where the device went.

scenes.title: The Vision of Ruin

mentor.speaker: Darth Miedo
mentor.text: A vision is information. Treating it as certainty is a different choice.

scenes.situation: A troubling Force vision suggests a distant research station may suffer a catastrophic failure. The symbols are ambiguous: you cannot tell whether you saw the future, a warning about the past or a deception. There is no confirmed crisis and no ready fleet to command.
scenes.question: What do you do with the warning?

answers.text: I investigate the symbols through records and other perspectives before deciding that the warning is literal.
I use whatever sensing power I already possess to learn whether the station faces danger now.
I move to the station to prepare its people for a possible failure while evidence is gathered.
I seek guidance through a Force tradition I have actually studied, comparing its teaching with my own judgment.

introCandidates.text: Corporate authority. A comforting phrase, until somebody asks you to make a decision. Your employer gives you access; it doesn't give you judgment. Are you here to lead people, build connections, or make competitors hesitate? Spare me the slogan.

questionCandidates.label: Core prompt
questionCandidates.text: As a Corporate Agent, what kind of professional influence do you want to develop?

answers.text: I want my people to hold steady when threats and intimidation threaten the work.
I want to give a trusted ally the chance to act when their judgment matters more than mine.
I want someone working beside me to stay ready even when danger catches everyone off guard.
I want my guidance to keep helping the team after I move away from them.
I want to restore the confidence of an ally who's hurting and close to giving up.
I want the people working together to make each other's efforts more effective.
I want my allies to seize an opening when an opponent tries to hurt one of us.
I want my presence to improve how effectively the people around me act.
I want one decisive move to bring the rest of my team into step.
I want to recognize the moment when a colleague can turn one critical effort into success.
I want several capable leaders to reinforce each other rather than issue competing directions.
I want the resources to build opportunities that last beyond a single contract.
I want broad knowledge that helps me recognize what matters in an unfamiliar business or negotiation.
I want useful contacts who can help when ordinary channels close their doors.
I want relationships with influential people who will listen when I need their help.
I want to draw on an unexpected skill when an assignment changes without warning.
I want to understand the technical side of an operation well enough to improve it when needed.
I want a network that can locate hard-to-find resources without making every request a public affair.
I want the resolve to reconsider a difficult decision and find a better result under pressure.
I want the people working with me to be ready to act the instant a negotiation turns dangerous.
I want to make an opponent rethink the value of fighting us, perhaps even accept a better arrangement.
I want my words to unsettle several opponents at once, costing them the time they need to act.
I want an entire group of adversaries to hesitate when I speak, giving my side a moment to respond.
I want the mental discipline to reject a single effort to intimidate or manipulate me.
I want someone who tries to hurt me to become more vulnerable to the pressure I apply next.
I want to learn how to give an ally a timely boost to their speed, accuracy, or defenses.
I want to protect the people affected by a corporation's decisions, even when doing so costs influence.
I want corporate leadership to be my destination, not a step toward another title.
I want to understand the different kinds of corporate influence before choosing how to use mine.

scenes.title: The Poisoned Contract

mentor.speaker: Marl Skindar
mentor.text: An offer that arrives just before the deadline is usually designed to keep you from reading it.

scenes.situation: A transport consortium offers a frontier community an urgent supply contract. Its price is attractive, but a hidden clause gives the consortium control over local warehouses if a shipment is late. Community representatives ask you to assess the deal; you do not own either organization.
scenes.question: What do you recommend?

answers.text: I examine the penalty clause and calculate exactly who carries the cost when deliveries fail.
I negotiate a smaller penalty and a shared inspection process before anyone signs.
I identify alternative suppliers so the community can bargain without depending on one bidder.
I convene both sides to set measurable delivery responsibilities and a way to resolve disputes.
I advise rejecting the contract until its terms can survive an open review, even if supplies arrive later.

scenes.title: The Rival Ledger

mentor.speaker: Marl Skindar
mentor.text: Someone adjusted the numbers. That is not yet proof that you know who.

scenes.situation: During an authorized review of a shipping cooperative, several inventory records conflict with actual deliveries. A rival firm has a motive, but two employees have made unexplained changes as well. The audit team has legitimate access to the ledgers, not to private messages or unrelated systems.
scenes.question: Where do you begin?

answers.text: I reconcile the physical shipment records with the ledger before accusing anyone of theft.
I speak separately with the clerks who handled the deliveries and look for contradictions.
I ask the systems staff to inspect the change history within the scope of the authorized audit.
I discreetly ask verified industry contacts whether the missing cargo appears in another market.
I secure the remaining stock and preserve the records so the supply chain stays functional during the inquiry.

scenes.title: The Meeting Without a Vote

mentor.speaker: Marl Skindar
mentor.text: The room is full of titles. None of them will do the thinking for you.

scenes.situation: At a tense emergency meeting, two departments refuse to share cargo space needed to deliver medical supplies. The directors have equal authority and the vote is tied. You have been asked to present a proposal, but you cannot order either department to comply.
scenes.question: How do you break the deadlock?

answers.text: I offer a shared schedule that gives each department a workable share of the cargo capacity.
I appeal to the directors' common responsibility for the patients waiting on those supplies.
I put the likely public and financial costs of delay on the record and demand an immediate decision.
I ask each director to name one nonnegotiable need, then build an agreement around those limits.
I secure a temporary smaller shipment now and plan a second delivery once the directors finish deliberating.

scenes.title: Assets on a Deadline

mentor.speaker: Marl Skindar
mentor.text: A fragile operation is one that needs every piece to behave exactly as the brochure promised.

scenes.situation: A manufacturing site is hours from missing a crucial shipment. A cooling unit has failed, a courier service has canceled, and the replacement budget is limited. You are acting as an outside consultant; the site manager may accept your plan but has not delegated control of the company.
scenes.question: What is your first priority?

answers.text: I ask the technicians to isolate the failed unit and see whether a safe temporary repair can keep production running.
I call qualified transport providers and compare their availability before committing more credits.
I reorganize the workload around the usable equipment instead of waiting for the broken unit.
I preserve the most time-sensitive materials and accept a partial delivery rather than destroy the whole batch.
I renegotiate the client deadline now, trading a concession for enough time to deliver safely.

scenes.title: The Public Statement

mentor.speaker: Marl Skindar
mentor.text: A public statement is easy. Living with the facts behind it is the difficult part.

scenes.situation: A local contractor is accused of selling faulty safety equipment. Independent tests are incomplete, a whistleblower fears retaliation, and a news network wants a statement immediately. The contractor's staff ask you to advise them. You have no automatic power to silence the press or dismiss employees.
scenes.question: What do you advise?

answers.text: I publish only the confirmed test results and clearly identify what remains unverified.
I arrange independent testing and delay any definitive claim until the results can withstand scrutiny.
I negotiate a public repair-and-compensation plan that the affected customers can actually verify.
I craft a narrow statement that protects the contractor's position while the inquiry proceeds.
I protect the whistleblower's identity and establish a trusted channel for further evidence.

introCandidates.text: Ah, the arena. I've seen a match teach the same lesson twice. Not many fighters enjoy the second one. You've reached the threshold; what would you rather master—staying alive, reading the next move, or giving the crowd something worth remembering?

questionCandidates.label: Core prompt
questionCandidates.text: As a Gladiator, what part of arena fighting do you want to make your own?

answers.text: I want armor to protect me without giving up the defenses I've earned through experience.
I want my skill and my armor to strengthen each other when the arena turns dangerous.
I want to move and defend myself naturally even in equipment that weighs me down.
I want to keep advancing in armor instead of letting it slow me at a critical moment.
I want to hold a shield's protection together when an opponent keeps pressing the attack.
I want the armor I wear to feel like another part of my fighting style.
I want to notice a shift in an opponent's stance before the real attack begins.
I want to follow an opponent's movements even when they try to shake me after a match.
I want to seize the first opening in a bout instead of waiting for my opponent to move.
I want to regain my timing when the rhythm of a fight turns against me.
I want to land a clean ranged strike even when smoke or poor visibility obscures the target.
I want to react when an opponent tries to catch me flat-footed.
I want to avoid being trapped between attackers who think they've found my blind spot.
I want to see where a formidable opponent's protection can actually be overcome.
I want to make a powerful hit count for more when it breaks through an opponent's endurance.
I want to single out a rival and make them pay for ignoring me to attack someone else.
I want a solid blow to leave an opponent more exposed to the next attack.
I want to handle strange arena weapons without treating each new one as a mystery.
I want to stop an opponent's movement the moment they try to get past me.
I want to make several attacks with an exotic weapon without losing the control each one requires.
I want a challenge from me to draw opponents' attention away from the people beside me.
I want to shake off one debilitating blow and keep fighting when a match should have ended.
I want to brace myself against a dangerous blow or attempt to break my will at the exact moment it matters.
I want to win contests through skill and showmanship, without needing to kill the person across from me.
I want to make gladiatorial mastery my destination rather than a step toward another title.
I want to learn which parts of arena fighting suit me before deciding what kind of champion to become.

scenes.title: The Bell Before the Strike

mentor.speaker: Pegar
mentor.text: The first three heartbeats tell you more than the last ten blows. Provided you are listening.

scenes.situation: At the start of an exhibition match, an opponent known for rushing across the sand advances immediately. You have space to move, an ordinary melee weapon and an agreed rule against attacking spectators. The opponent has not yet committed to a specific strike.
scenes.question: How do you open the exchange?

answers.text: I watch the opponent's feet and shoulders until their first move reveals where they are vulnerable.
I step forward with a hard opening attack before they can settle into their charge.
I brace behind my protection and make them spend their momentum against a prepared defense.
I shift to the side and let the rushing fighter overcommit before I answer.
I call out a challenge and try to make the opponent focus on me instead of changing targets.

scenes.title: The Unfamiliar Weapon

mentor.speaker: Pegar
mentor.text: I once won with a weapon I could not name. The important part was learning what end to hold.

scenes.situation: An arena exhibition uses unfamiliar equipment. A long hooked blade, a heavy shield, a short staff and a weighted net lie at separate markers. You may reach one before your opponent closes, but none is a weapon you have been promised proficiency with.
scenes.question: What do you do?

answers.text: I choose the strange hooked blade and test its balance rather than shy away from an unfamiliar weapon.
I take the shield and make the opponent work to find an opening before committing to attack.
I reach for the net and try to limit the opponent's movement before closing in.
I stay mobile and use the markers as obstacles while I judge which weapon the opponent fears most.
I take the simple staff and concentrate on precise, repeatable strikes rather than spectacular ones.

scenes.title: Two Against One

mentor.speaker: Pegar
mentor.text: Three fighters in the sand. That means three stories. Make certain you are still in yours at the end.

scenes.situation: A three-contender arena bout begins with two rivals moving toward you from different angles. The rules allow temporary cooperation, but no side has agreed to an alliance. The open floor has one raised platform and no reliable cover.
scenes.question: How do you keep the encounter manageable?

answers.text: I move to the platform so only one opponent can approach me cleanly at a time.
I concentrate on the more aggressive rival and try to put them down before the other can engage.
I call out the more cautious contender and attempt to draw their attention while keeping the other in sight.
I offer a temporary truce to the opponent who seems least committed to fighting me.
I conserve my strength, defend against both angles and wait for the rivals to expose each other.

scenes.title: The Fallen Contender

mentor.speaker: Pegar
mentor.text: The crowd never walks home with your wounds. Remember that when it starts shouting.

scenes.situation: An opponent falls to one knee in an exhibition. Their weapon lies within reach, but they have not surrendered. The audience demands a finishing blow, and the official will stop the match if either combatant clearly signals a surrender. The opponent is watching your next step.
scenes.question: How do you handle the moment?

answers.text: I demand that the opponent surrender and keep enough distance to prevent a desperate attack.
I move to secure the loose weapon before committing to another exchange.
I hold my stance and let the official confirm whether the fight is continuing.
I press the advantage with a controlled strike, knowing the opponent still has a chance to fight back.
I offer the opponent a clear way to yield and make the official hear it over the crowd.

scenes.title: The Changing Arena

mentor.speaker: Pegar
mentor.text: Some arenas have a habit of trying to fight you too. I always respected that.

scenes.situation: Midway through a public match, floor plates rise, smoke vents open and the fighting area narrows to a rotating platform. Your opponent knows the hazards only as well as you do. The environmental machinery is controlled by officials beyond the ring.
scenes.question: How do you adapt?

answers.text: I spend a moment studying the new cycle so I can move when the floor is most stable.
I stay close to the opponent and deny them the space they need to exploit the rotating platform.

I use my armor and guard to absorb the worst of the disruption until a safe opening appears.
I launch one decisive attack when the opponent loses footing instead of matching every shift of the floor.

introCandidates.text: A duel is not won by reputation. It is decided by distance, timing, and the choices made when another fighter moves. You have earned the chance to study this craft. Which part will you train until it no longer demands thought?

questionCandidates.label: Core prompt
questionCandidates.text: As a Melee Duelist, what kind of close-combat expertise do you want to perfect?

answers.text: I want to keep pressure on an opponent until they can no longer dictate the pace of our exchange.

I want a forceful unarmed strike to stagger an opponent rather than simply wound them.
I want to upset an opponent's footing and make their next attack less dependable.
I want to keep my footing and protect myself when several enemies crowd into reach.
I want taking away an enemy's weapon to create an immediate close-combat opening.
I want to turn a physically stronger opponent's efforts against them in a close struggle.
I want a precise attack to separate an opponent from the weapon they trust.
I want the weapon I've practiced with to deliver more decisive blows.
I want a penetrating strike to make it harder for an opponent to ignore the wound.
I want the ability to suppress an opponent effectively when my equipment and tactics call for ranged fire.
I want a well-placed attack to leave an opponent feeling its effect after the initial hit.
I want a heavy strike to overwhelm someone who thought they could absorb it.
I want my chosen weapon to make a tough opponent more likely to feel the full force of a hit.
I want to get a strike through defenses that would blunt a less practiced attack.
I want to use sustained fire when a close-combat duel turns into a larger engagement.
I want to punish the instant an opponent moves carelessly within my reach.
I want to feint quickly enough that my opponent has less time to read my next strike.
I want the opening created by one blade to let my second blade strike the same opponent.
I want two-weapon attacks to become fast enough that I can commit to a full exchange without losing the moment.
I want precise handwork and agility, rather than brute strength, to put force behind a light blade.
I want to deliver several blows with an advanced melee weapon without sacrificing control.
I want a successful feint to lead immediately into a surprise strike with my blade.
I want to move freely through a duel even while committing to multiple strikes with one blade.
I want a full sequence of strikes with one blade to fit into the opening most opponents would use for a single attack.
I want difficult terrain and obstacles to stop deciding where I can move in a duel.
I want the discipline to meet a formidable opponent alone without relying on spectacle or an audience.
I want to perfect the art of the duel for its own sake, without needing another title.
I want to understand the different approaches to close combat before choosing the style I will perfect.

scenes.title: The First Opening

mentor.speaker: Blade Master Kharjo
mentor.text: Distance is a decision. The first fighter to ignore that has already yielded something.

scenes.situation: A challenger with a heavy vibroblade faces you on a narrow bridge above an empty drainage channel. Both have room to advance but little room to circle. The challenger lowers their shoulder as if preparing a committed attack. Neither has struck yet.
scenes.question: How do you take the opening?

I close before their swing reaches full force and drive a precise strike into their guard.
I feint toward the centerline to draw their blade away from the lane I intend to use.
I aim to disarm the challenger rather than trade heavy blows on a narrow bridge.
I give ground to wider footing and refuse a duel on terrain chosen by the challenger.

scenes.title: The Second Blade

mentor.speaker: Blade Master Kharjo
mentor.text: Two weapons do not make twice the fighter. They make twice the rhythm to study.

scenes.situation: At a training tournament, a rival uses two short blades and alternates quick feints with coordinated attacks. You may choose how to answer using the weapons you are actually proficient with. The practice bout ends with a touch, disarm or agreed yield.
scenes.question: Which method do you practice?

answers.text: I match their two-blade rhythm with a pair of my own, working toward a coordinated combination.
I keep one blade and use space efficiently, waiting until the opponent overextends.
I attack the weapon hand with a disarming motion when the two blades cross.
I move outside the paired attacks and force the rival to turn before they can strike together.

scenes.title: The Weapon Taken

mentor.speaker: Blade Master Kharjo
mentor.text: A lost weapon is a fact. Panic is an addition you make yourself.

scenes.situation: During a practice challenge in a workshop, an opponent hooks your weapon away. It slides behind a workbench. Your opponent is advancing, and nearby are a loose tool handle, a length of cable and a doorway to open ground. The fight remains a controlled sparring exercise.
scenes.question: How do you continue?

answers.text: I use the tool handle as an improvised weapon and maintain enough range to keep fighting.
I close into a grapple so the opponent's reach matters less than control of their arms.
I move through the doorway and recover distance before retrieving my weapon.
I fake a rush, then dart around the workbench to recover the weapon while their guard shifts.
I take the immediate defensive stance and wait for a chance to counter or disarm their own weapon.

scenes.title: The False Courtesy

mentor.speaker: Blade Master Kharjo
mentor.text: The rules may change. Your discipline should not have to vanish with them.

scenes.situation: In a formal exhibition, your opponent agreed to fight without outside equipment. Halfway through, they draw a concealed shock device and the referee has not yet noticed. The audience believes the bout remains fair. You can signal the official, change tactics or continue, but no one has declared you champion.
scenes.question: What do you do?

answers.text: I alert the referee and keep a safe guard until the device can be removed from the bout.
I use the opponent's moment of concealment as the opening for a swift, precise counterattack.
I try to disarm the shock device before it can be used against me.
I break their rhythm with a convincing feint and make them expose the device in plain sight.
I retreat to open space and refuse to remain in range of the device until I understand what it does.

scenes.title: The Corridor of Obstacles

mentor.speaker: Blade Master Kharjo
mentor.text: A perfect technique in an empty room is only half a technique.

scenes.situation: Inside a crowded repair corridor, a hostile fighter advances with a long cutting weapon. Workers are retreating through a narrow hatch behind you, while loose crates and conduits block a straight line of movement. You have no automatic authority over the workers.
scenes.question: How do you resolve the approach?

answers.text: I move around the crates to draw the attacker away from the hatch before closing in.
I hold the narrow approach and make the attacker come through my blade's best distance.
I press into close quarters, where the attacker's long weapon will be harder to maneuver.
I attempt a fast disarm so the workers can finish retreating without a prolonged duel.
I use the loose crates as a diversion, forcing the attacker to change direction before I strike.

introCandidates.text: Got an organization behind you. Fine. That means nothing if you can't handle the next problem. You want to track somebody down, bring them in, or make sure they don't try anything? Pick what works.

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Enforcer, which kind of investigative or enforcement expertise do you intend to develop?

answers.text: I want to evade the worst of an explosion or other area attack when I cannot get clear.
I want a brief surge of strength when lifting an obstacle or carrying someone to safety demands it.
I want to close the distance on a fleeing suspect before they disappear into the crowd.
I want rough ground and obstacles to slow me less when someone needs to be reached.
I want to disable a suspect's vehicle with a calculated ram without sacrificing my own vehicle.
I want to run a twisting chase route without losing speed every time it changes direction.
I want reliable stun techniques that let me take a dangerous suspect alive.
I want my standing to earn cooperation from people who would otherwise keep their distance.
I want to bring automatic fire under control quickly when cover is available.
I want a stunning attack to hinder a suspect's escape as well as wear them down.
I want a charge to put a resisting opponent on the ground before they can recover.

This work is the calling I earned. I want to become exceptional at it without needing another title.

scenes.title: The Moving Suspect

mentor.speaker: Krag the Immovable
mentor.text: Fast feet are useful. A good head tells you where to put them.

scenes.situation: A suspect carrying stolen access credentials runs through a busy transit market. They have not threatened anyone, but reaching the platform could let them disappear into a departing crowd. Two security volunteers offer help; you do not command them automatically.
scenes.question: How do you respond?

answers.text: I follow the suspect through the crowd and adjust my route so I do not lose them at the platform.
I ask the volunteers to watch the exits and report movement instead of all joining the chase.
I watch the suspect's habits and try to predict which entrance they will choose next.
I cut across a safer side street and try to reach the platform before the suspect.
I alert transit security and provide the suspect's description before the train arrives.

scenes.title: The Stun Window

mentor.speaker: Krag the Immovable
mentor.text: A living suspect can answer questions. A bystander in the line of fire cannot. Keep both in mind.

scenes.situation: A desperate saboteur backs into a maintenance bay with a charged blaster. A mechanic is sheltering behind a low crate, and the saboteur is still looking for an exit. Stun equipment may be available only if the character or local security actually possesses it.
scenes.question: How do you contain the threat?

answers.text: I use an available stun setting or weapon to stop the saboteur without needing a lethal shot.
