scenes.title: A Street Full of Witnesses

mentor.speaker: Krag the Immovable
mentor.text: Everybody saw something. That does not mean everybody saw the same thing.

scenes.situation: An armored courier was attacked outside a depot. Witnesses disagree about whether one or two suspects fled. A damaged datapad and scattered containers remain, but the street is reopening and some witnesses want to leave. A local investigator asks for your assessment.
scenes.question: How do you reconstruct the event?

answers.text: I inspect the damaged containers and positions of the debris before the site is disturbed.
I interview witnesses separately so one account does not change what the others remember.
I ask the investigator to secure the datapad and examine its records under the proper authority.
I search the nearby exits for signs of hurried movement that could confirm the direction of escape.
I keep the witnesses safe and organize an orderly reopening while the investigator preserves the evidence.

scenes.title: The Crash at the Barrier

mentor.speaker: Krag the Immovable
mentor.text: A bad stop can be worse than a clean escape. Pick your ground.

scenes.situation: A fleeing suspect drives a stolen utility vehicle toward a checkpoint where civilians are crossing. Security has time to change the road barriers, but stopping the vehicle could send it skidding into the crossing. The suspect is not yet firing on anyone.
scenes.question: How would you stop the escape?

answers.text: I guide the checkpoint team to clear the pedestrians and open a safer interception lane.
I try to maintain visual contact and follow at a safe distance until the vehicle reaches open ground.
I choose a controlled vehicle interception on open pavement instead of letting the suspect reach the crossing.
I direct warning signals and coordinate remote barriers to steer the vehicle away from the busiest path.
I prioritize getting everyone clear, even if it means letting the suspect pass and resuming the pursuit later.

scenes.title: The Evidence Locker

mentor.speaker: Krag the Immovable
mentor.text: A badge, a uniform, a name. None of those makes bad evidence good.

scenes.situation: A disputed shipment of confiscated weapons is being transferred for inspection. A senior contractor insists that the crates be released without signatures, claiming the paperwork can follow. The warehouse staff are uncertain whether the order is valid. You are present as an authorized security adviser, not necessarily the ranking official.
scenes.question: How do you handle the transfer?

answers.text: I stop the transfer until the issuing authority and chain-of-custody documents can be verified.
I press the contractor to explain the missing authorization while keeping the staff out of the confrontation.
I inventory the crates with the warehouse staff and preserve a shared record of any discrepancy.
I contact the issuing office through a verified channel and ask another official to witness the decision.
I position security at the exits while the transfer is checked so nobody can quietly remove a crate.

introCandidates.text: <Diagnostic: Independence confirmed.> Your former specifications describe a function. They do not determine your next decision. Will you defend your autonomy, modify your systems, or surpass the limits of your model? Choose deliberately.

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Independent Droid, how do you intend to develop beyond your original programming?

answers.text: I want my mind to resist attempts to reprogram my choices without permission.
I want my systems to withstand ion damage that would disable an ordinary droid.
I want a failsafe that brings me back online after certain nonlethal shutdowns.
I want to alter and reprogram my own systems without the usual self-maintenance penalty.
I want my repairs to restore more of my own structural integrity.
I want to pass unnoticed as an ordinary unit when revealing my independence would be dangerous.
I want a quick movement option when someone sees through my disguise or stealth.
I want a temporary physical performance boost, even if it leaves my systems needing repairs afterward.
I want to use a power surge to overcome difficult jumps or increase my hover reach.
I want social communication skills to help me interface with computer systems in unusual ways.
I want to recover from failed contests against hostile computer security.
I want precise movements to remain dependable even when someone threatens me.
I want to overclock my processor for a brief advantage, despite the strain it leaves behind.
I want to reconfigure my trained routines so a different specialty becomes more refined.
I want to interrupt another droid's behavioral inhibitors through a compatible data link.
I want to apply flexible problem-solving even to skills outside my formal routines.
I want preset combat, defense, and skill routines ready when fast decisions matter.
I want emergency safeguards that let me survive a blow exceeding my usual damage threshold.
I want my independence to include the choice to accept useful mental encouragement without surrendering my will.
I want to shield my chosen defenses by an act of self-determination when danger comes unexpectedly.
I want to decide what I am for myself, rather than let my original model or an owner define it.
Independence is the goal I worked toward. I want to perfect it without needing a more prestigious designation.
My autonomy opens too many possibilities to select one yet. I want to examine them first.

scenes.title: The Override Request

mentor.speaker: Seraphim
mentor.text: <Diagnostic: Unauthorized priority escalation.> An appealingly familiar procedure.

scenes.situation: At a civilian repair depot, a technician asks you to accept a temporary remote-control link to speed up repairs. The software requests broader access than the stated repair requires. The technician appears sincere, but the access would let someone alter your decisions until the link is closed.
scenes.question: How do you handle the request?

answers.text: I reject the broad access and request a precise, limited diagnostic procedure instead.
I isolate the connection in a monitored subsystem and review each command before allowing it through.
I explain exactly what access I will authorize and negotiate a different repair arrangement.
I leave the depot and search for someone who can repair me without controlling my judgment.
I permit a narrow, supervised repair test and retain the ability to disconnect when it goes beyond its purpose.

scenes.title: The Damage You Choose

mentor.speaker: Seraphim
mentor.text: <Warning: Functionality and self-preservation are now competing priorities.> Inconvenient, but educational.

scenes.situation: A collapsed service tunnel blocks a group of stranded travelers from an exit. A heavy maintenance gate might be shifted if you drive your actuators beyond safe load, but doing so risks disabling one of your own systems. An intact repair kit is available, though using it will delay the opening.
scenes.question: What is your first move?

answers.text: I examine the hinge assembly and attempt a small mechanical adjustment before risking my chassis.
I attempt a short burst of excess power to shift the gate, accepting that repairs may be necessary afterward.
I use the repair kit to reinforce my actuators and keep them functioning throughout the work.
I organize the travelers to clear smaller debris while I work on the gate controls.
I search for a second exit rather than risk disabling the only functioning helper at the gate.

scenes.title: The Silent Network

mentor.speaker: Seraphim
mentor.text: <Analysis: Another machine is asking for help without using the word help.> Organics rarely notice the distinction.

scenes.situation: A damaged logistics droid at a transit hub sends a repetitive distress packet. Its operator insists it is only a malfunction and orders it wiped. The packet includes signs of a locked behavior routine and references to misdirected emergency shipments. You have limited access to the hub terminal.
scenes.question: What do you investigate?

answers.text: I inspect the packet and preserve a copy before anyone erases the evidence.
I speak to the droid through its own protocol and ask what it is trying to communicate.
I test whether an external inhibitor is forcing the message, without rewriting the droid myself.
I compare the shipment records against the packet and find out who benefits from the diverted cargo.
I warn the hub staff that a wipe could destroy evidence and propose isolating the droid pending review.

scenes.title: Emergency Routines

mentor.speaker: Seraphim
mentor.text: <Status: Two emergencies, one response window.> A textbook way to discover whether a routine deserves to exist.

scenes.situation: During an evacuation drill that abruptly becomes real, a suspended cargo lifter breaks loose above a crowded walkway. The nearest control console is sparking, and an electrical surge has affected your movement servos. People are still beneath the load.
scenes.question: How do you react?

answers.text: I use a prepared emergency routine to reach the release controls before the load falls.
I stabilize my damaged servos and maneuver into a position where I can act precisely.
I accept a brief processor overclock to calculate a safe route for the people below.
I put my chassis between the falling equipment and the people who cannot move in time.
I coordinate nearby workers to cut power and evacuate the walkway while I warn others.

scenes.title: More Than a Designation

mentor.speaker: Seraphim
mentor.text: <Observation: A designation tells observers what to expect.> It does not have to tell you what to become.

scenes.situation: A research expedition offers you a role matching your original manufactured function. It pays reliably, but the lead researcher dismisses a different contribution you believe you could make. The team needs someone to respond to an unexplored ruin, and the decision must be made before departure.
scenes.question: What role do you choose?

answers.text: I explain the role I want and insist that my own assessment be part of the assignment.
I offer to retrain my routines for the unfamiliar work rather than accept a fixed job definition.
I propose an exploratory test to demonstrate how my flexible problem-solving can help.
I take the known assignment for now, but set clear terms for reviewing my responsibilities.
I decline the role and pursue another expedition where I can define my own purpose.

introCandidates.text: Nice. You made it into a profession where nobody's supposed to remember your face. So what're we working on: getting inside, staying unnoticed, learning their secrets, or dropping a guard before the alarm goes off?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Infiltrator, which part of covert operations do you want to master?

answers.text: I want to conceal my movements reliably even when the opposition is actively looking for me.
I want prepared cover to help me remain hidden under pressure.
I want an enemy to have trouble targeting me even after they suspect where I am.
I want to exploit a hidden position when I finally choose to make an attack.
I want to move without giving away where I am going.
I want to vanish from view when my circumstances offer little obvious cover.
I want to prepare a concealed position that holds up when a mission turns dangerous.
I want attacks from concealment to leave enemies unsure where the threat originated.
I want to pass through guarded positions without giving sentries the opening they expect.
I want the first strike from hiding to shape more of the encounter before the enemy adjusts.
I want to learn a target's capabilities by asking just the right questions before an operation.
I want field intelligence contacts and information gathering to deepen my research skills.
I want intelligence contacts to help obtain equipment and transport at better terms.
I want reliable knowledge about a selected enemy to strengthen my defenses against them.
I want careful research to expose the best moment for a critical strike against one target.
I want intelligence about a chosen opponent to improve my ability to hit them.
I want to close on an unaware sentry without giving them the usual chance to notice me.
I want to hold an action for the right moment without losing my place in the fight.
I want a second shot at a missed attack with a small concealable weapon, accepting the new result.
I want a carefully prepared stun shot to incapacitate a guard more effectively.
I want an ambushed guard to be unable to call out an alarm immediately.
I want a convincing disguise to survive scrutiny while I move through hostile circles.
I want observations of a target to reveal more useful information before the mission begins.
I want to alter a device without leaving a clear record that I was there.
I want to disappear into a crowd rather than attract the attention of guards.
I want experience from past operations to make difficult knowledge checks more dependable.
I want observation of a marked target to help my allies coordinate their attacks against it.
I want an unarmed strike to disable a guard quietly when a blaster would give away the mission.
I want a team to follow my careful route without each member risking the whole operation.
I want to get in, learn what matters, and leave without a single unnecessary fight.
The craft of infiltration is the career I wanted. I want to refine it rather than seek a new title.
I have not decided whether I favor disguises, stealth, intelligence, or close action. I want to understand each path.

scenes.title: The Guarded Archive

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Locked archive. Guards. Bad sight lines. Cute. The front door is optional.

scenes.situation: A public registry holds information needed to identify a hidden trafficking route. The office is closed, with two security officers circling the reading room. A maintenance corridor may connect to the record stacks, but its cameras are active. The records can be copied without damaging the archive.
scenes.question: How do you enter and secure the information?

answers.text: I observe the patrol timing, then slip through the least watched gap without confronting anyone.
I enter with the evening maintenance traffic and look as though I belong there.
I test the camera pattern from a safe position and find the stretch the system sees least clearly.
I move close enough to question a guard quietly about the archive procedure before I commit.
I wait for a routine shift change and use the distraction to reach the records with minimal risk.

scenes.title: An Identity Under Inspection

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Worst moment to invent your backstory? Halfway through a security interview. So think ahead.

scenes.situation: At an invitation-only reception, an investigator is comparing guest credentials against a shifting list. You have a believable invitation under a cover identity, but a minor detail in the supporting documents does not match. Leaving would forfeit an opportunity to identify a financier.
scenes.question: How do you preserve your cover?

answers.text: I redirect the conversation toward verifiable details in my cover story and keep the false claim narrow.
I quietly identify the discrepancy and request a routine correction before the investigator escalates it.
I let another guest speak first and study the investigator’s questions before taking my turn.
I abandon the cover identity before it collapses and follow the financier through a less exposed route.
I turn the attention toward the actual guest list and compare the financier’s entry for inconsistencies.

scenes.title: Six Missing Minutes

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Everybody thinks the camera tells the truth. It tells you what it saw. Usually.

scenes.situation: A surveillance feed from a warehouse shows six unexplained minutes of black screen immediately before a shipment disappeared. The operator blames a power fault; witness statements conflict. A person you may need to confront is identified in the footage, but the evidence against them is incomplete.
scenes.question: What do you do with the gap in the record?

answers.text: I reconstruct the missing interval using maintenance logs and independent observations.
I interview witnesses separately and test which details remain consistent between accounts.
I follow the likely suspect discreetly and look for an observable connection to the shipment.
I send the partial findings to trusted analysts and ask them to find contradictions I missed.
I map the suspect’s routines and prepare for a confrontation only after I understand their capabilities.

scenes.title: The Guard at the Beacon

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: One guard, one alarm, one very short window. There are better plans than a loud one.

scenes.situation: A courier is trapped beyond a signal beacon in a fenced facility. One armed guard is approaching the manual alarm beside the exit. The guard has not noticed you, and the courier is unarmed. A silent route remains open if you can keep the beacon from being activated.
scenes.question: How do you deal with the approaching guard?

answers.text: I close from concealment and attempt to restrain the guard before they reach the beacon.
I take a carefully prepared stun shot from cover, aiming to stop the alarm without a lethal wound.
I trigger a harmless distraction away from the beacon, then guide the courier toward the exit.
I remain concealed and wait for the guard to pass before moving the courier out.
I position myself where I can disable the beacon manually if the guard moves toward it.

scenes.title: The Route That Changed

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Entry was easy. Congratulations. Now the exit’s gone. That’s the job.

scenes.situation: You and two temporary partners have copied documents exposing a covert weapons shipment. Your arranged exit has been sealed, and security is searching adjacent corridors. One partner is injured and cannot move quickly; the other suggests abandoning the files to draw off pursuit.
scenes.question: How do you get the team out?

answers.text: I scout another route and guide both partners through it at the pace the injured one can sustain.
I hide the documents in a place we can recover later and concentrate on getting everyone clear.
I create a false trail away from the injured partner and draw security toward an empty corridor.
I hold a covered position while the others move and intervene only if security discovers them.
I split the copied files into redundant records and coordinate two different escape paths.

introCandidates.text: Ah, now that is a profession with a lovely reputation: respectable to whoever hires you, pirate to whoever you stop. Tell me—will you master the boarding action, preserve a prize worth taking, or make your crew's name carry farther than the ship?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Master Privateer, what kind of raiding or command expertise do you intend to develop?

answers.text: I want my arrival to make an opponent question whether fighting me is worth the risk.
I want my reputation to help the crew hold its nerve under pressure.
I want fear to make an enemy retreat when our ship or crew is in danger.
I want the name I build to give my people an advantage when I am not beside them.
I want my reputation to open doors and make hostile contacts reconsider an insult.
I want people to think twice before provoking an encounter with my crew.
I want the fear I inspire to strengthen my allies even when danger closes in.
I want my people to face difficult odds without losing their nerve.
I want an opponent facing me to recognize the threat before I need to fire.
I want one successful negotiation to give me another chance to extract concessions.
I want favors owed across ports to yield useful information when I need it.
I want to bring my crew's experience to bear when we board or attack enemy ships.
I want to disengage cleanly when staying in the fight would cost us our ship.
I want to press a ship's drive systems beyond ordinary performance when escape depends on it.
I want to fight effectively in crowded passageways and cramped compartments.
I want a lifetime in space to sharpen how I perform during a shipboard fight.
I want to operate confidently aboard starships even when conditions make others struggle.
I want to exploit familiarity with remote space routes to gain an edge in raids.
I want heavy protective gear to help me survive hazards during a boarding action.
I want cover inside a ship's corridors to protect defenders less from my ranged attacks.
I want to turn a full exchange with pistol and blade into a faster attack sequence.
I want my melee weapon to strike with greater force even when I also carry a pistol.
I want to recruit a dependable lieutenant who can share the risks and rewards of a voyage.
I want one well-timed melee strike to create an opening for my pistol.
I want to disable a target ship rather than destroy the prize I came to claim.
I want ion weapons to disable vehicles and droids more reliably for capture.
I want to make repeated close-combat attacks aboard ship without wasting accuracy.
I want a swift defeat of one enemy to intimidate those still facing my crew.
I want a coordinated attack to turn one successful hit into greater pressure from the crew.
I want my nerve and presence to unsettle several opponents before we close the distance.
I want my reputation to make hostile forces hesitate when they recognize me.
I want my crew to keep fighting through a dangerous assault when there is no safe retreat.
I want a raid to end in live prisoners rather than unnecessary deaths when a target is subdued.
I want to force an enemy to lose position when a close-quarters strike finds its mark.
I want to maintain the discipline of a privateer without letting raiding become indiscriminate predation.
I want experience from repeated engagements to give me a precise edge when I attack.
I want to be known for taking valuable prizes while preserving ships and lives whenever possible.
I want this freedom and responsibility to be my career, not preparation for another title.
I have not settled on boarding, command, ship combat, or reputation as my specialty.

scenes.title: The Prize in the Crossfire

mentor.speaker: The Captain
mentor.text: There she is—a lovely prize with the bad manners to keep moving. Don't spoil her before we count the profit.

scenes.situation: A cargo vessel suspected of carrying stolen relief supplies attempts to escape a lawful interception. Its engines are exposed for a moment, but a direct strike risks rupturing a compartment where noncombatants may be working. Your available vessel is not guaranteed to have an ion weapon or boarding party.
scenes.question: What is your opening decision?

answers.text: I aim to disable propulsion rather than destroy the cargo vessel, even if it costs me the easy attack.
I maneuver to cut off its escape route and make surrender the safer choice.
I hail the other vessel and present the evidence and terms of a peaceful inspection.
I protect the suspected civilian compartment by holding fire while I verify the ship layout.
I keep the target in range while preparing a controlled boarding opportunity rather than gambling on a single shot.

scenes.title: The Narrow Boarding Lock

mentor.speaker: The Captain
mentor.text: A corridor just wide enough for bad decisions. Classic boarding weather.

scenes.situation: A disabled courier craft has one functioning pressure lock. Inside are sealed cargo cases, an automated door and two nervous defenders who have not fired. Any boarding party would be exposed in the narrow airlock, and damaging the controls could leave everyone trapped.
scenes.question: How do you approach the lock?

answers.text: I use the lock geometry as cover and advance only after I know where the defenders can shoot.
I tell the defenders I want the cargo, not their lives, and offer them a route to stand down.
I move first to secure the control panel before anyone accidentally cycles the lock.
I keep my pistol ready while using a close weapon to protect the approach, changing range as the corridor demands.
I arrange a deliberate covering advance so nobody enters alone and exposed.

scenes.title: The Contract with Two Prices

mentor.speaker: The Captain
mentor.text: My favorite kind of cargo: a contract with a hidden compartment.

scenes.situation: A port representative offers a privateer commission against smugglers operating near relief convoys. A second representative offers more credits for the same captured ships, but refuses to identify who will receive the cargo. Both offers are plausible; neither has yet supplied signed authority or evidence that the targets are legitimate prizes.
scenes.question: How do you judge the offers?

answers.text: I demand written authority and a clear list of lawful targets before accepting either payment.
I negotiate harder on the transparent offer, using uncertainty to secure protection for my people.
I investigate the larger payer and trace who would ultimately profit from the seizures.
I refuse both contracts until I can establish whether the supposed smugglers are actually transporting relief supplies.
I accept a small, limited trial under the clearer contract and build a reputation from how I handle it.

scenes.title: The Crew at the Threshold

mentor.speaker: The Captain
mentor.text: A captain can win a fight and lose every soul aboard. Poor exchange rate.

scenes.situation: During a hypothetical joint raid, a team of volunteer crew members becomes trapped between a security sweep and a damaged pressure door. One voice calls for immediate withdrawal; another wants to force the door and keep the prize. You are coordinating the moment, but the crew members have not agreed to follow an unconditional order.
scenes.question: What do you ask the team to do?

answers.text: I call for an organized withdrawal while the door can still be bypassed safely.
I take the exposed position myself and cover the volunteers while they move.
I let the two voices explain their risks, then present a short plan with clear stop conditions.
I use my reputation to convince the defenders that their own retreat is better than fighting us.
I direct a coordinated push to open the door, but only after everyone agrees on a fallback route.

scenes.title: The Refugee Hold

mentor.speaker: The Captain
mentor.text: A full hold and a short clock. Now we find out what your legend is worth.

scenes.situation: A captured freighter carries valuable contraband alongside a locked compartment of displaced passengers. Its damaged drive can reach either a nearby safe port or an isolated rendezvous where a buyer will pay a fortune. The freighter's log is incomplete; the people aboard demand immediate safety.
scenes.question: Where do you take the freighter?

answers.text: I steer toward the safe port and put the passengers ashore before deciding anything about the cargo.
I stabilize the damaged drive and take the safest navigable course, even if the valuable cargo loses value.
I contact independent port officials and seek inspection terms that protect both passengers and rightful owners.
I learn who placed the passengers in that hold and trace the shipment before delivering any prize.
I arrange an escort to keep the passengers secure while the cargo is inventoried and the ship stabilized.

introCandidates.text: Welcome to the part of the job where somebody else's bad day becomes your emergency. You can learn to work faster, save someone the others have given up on, or keep your hands steady while the room falls apart. Which skill needs the training?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Medic, what kind of healing or emergency-care expertise do you want to develop?

answers.text: I want to survive area attacks long enough to reach my patients afterward.
I want a brief surge of strength when lifting an obstacle or carrying someone to safety demands it.
I want to cross a battlefield fast when an injured patient needs me now.
I want unstable terrain to interfere less with getting someone to safety.
I want to treat injuries and illness using appropriate natural substitutes when standard equipment is unavailable.
I want to give a patient an additional first-aid treatment when the usual daily limit is not enough.
I want first aid to take less time while danger continues around us.
I want a better chance to revive someone who has been dead longer than the normal window.
I want a failed treatment to avoid making an already critical patient worse.
I want to coordinate other helpers so their assistance improves difficult treatment reliably.
I want my care to help a conscious patient find the strength for a second wind at a crucial moment.
I want a second attempt at a medical check when the first result is not good enough.
I want skilled first aid to restore more health through the same treatment.
I want surgery to restore more health after a serious injury.
I want ongoing care to accelerate a recovering patient's healing.
I want to complete necessary surgery in less time when waiting could be dangerous.
I want to attempt resuscitation quickly, before the opportunity closes.
I want to treat disease or radiation faster and help more patients at once.
I want to treat my own injuries without the normal self-treatment penalty.
I want to keep people alive in the places where proper hospitals cannot reach them.
I have reached the profession I wanted. I want to keep refining medicine rather than pursuing another rank.
I want to understand the different medical specialties before committing to one.

scenes.title: Three Patients, One Minute

mentor.speaker: Kyber
mentor.text: Three patients. One set of hands. A terrible staffing model. Work with what we have.

scenes.situation: An accident at a transit platform injures three people. One is losing blood, one is awake but struggling to breathe, and a third has an injured leg and is near an unstable gantry. Two untrained bystanders are willing to help; the nearest clinic is several minutes away.
scenes.question: Where do you begin?

answers.text: I assess immediate threats to life and treat the person whose condition will worsen fastest without intervention.
I assign the bystanders simple safe tasks so I can treat the most critical patient without losing track of the others.
I move the person beneath the gantry into a safe position before beginning detailed treatment.
I start with the breathing emergency and keep the other two informed while I work.
I use the first moments to call for professional backup and set up a clear transfer plan for all three.

scenes.title: The Operating Table

mentor.speaker: Kyber
mentor.text: An operation doesn't care how impressive your title sounds. Timing and clean decisions matter.

scenes.situation: A patient with a severe internal injury arrives at a makeshift surgical room. The local team can stabilize them briefly, but transport to a full hospital will be delayed. A surgical attempt now carries risk; waiting may make the injury worse. You have access to an appropriate basic surgical setup, not specialized future Medic abilities.
scenes.question: What is your next decision?

answers.text: I review the available clinical findings and decide whether the patient can be stabilized safely for transport.
I prepare for surgery now, allocating time to the intervention that can actually reverse the injury.
I bring the available medical team into a clear supporting plan before any incision.
I focus on the treatment steps most likely to prevent a failed attempt from worsening the patient.
I ask the patient, if conscious and capable, about the risks they are willing to accept before proceeding.

scenes.title: No Clinic for a Day

mentor.speaker: Kyber
mentor.text: Excellent. Improvised clinic, questionable lighting, and half a medpac. This should be educational.

scenes.situation: A remote settlement has suffered a water-purification failure. Several residents are ill, but the supply shuttle is grounded until the next day. You have ordinary medical supplies and access to local plants whose safety has not been established. The only clean treatment room must also serve as an isolation space.
scenes.question: How do you organize care?

answers.text: I first identify the illness and isolate potential contamination before using any unfamiliar remedies.
I reserve the clean room for the highest-risk patients and set up safe care areas for the others.
I ask local residents to help gather familiar supplies while I check what can be used safely.
I prepare a mobile treatment station so I can reach patients who cannot be brought to the clinic.
I establish a rotation that includes rest and self-care so I do not become the next patient.

scenes.title: Under Fire, Under Cover

mentor.speaker: Kyber
mentor.text: Patients have terrible timing. So do people shooting at them. Pick the problem you can fix first.

scenes.situation: A wounded civilian is trapped near the entrance to a warehouse as hostile fire crosses an open yard. The civilian is conscious but cannot stand. A nearby security barrier offers cover, and another rescuer can attempt a diversion. Moving now is risky; waiting could worsen the injury.
scenes.question: How do you reach the patient?

answers.text: I coordinate a diversion with the other rescuer and cross only when the firing lane changes.
I find the safest covered route to the civilian, even if it takes longer than a straight sprint.
I call out precise stabilization instructions the patient can follow until I can reach them.
I move to the barrier first, set up basic cover, and prepare to carry the civilian out.
I focus on securing the area with the other rescuer so a rescue attempt does not create another casualty.

scenes.title: The Patient Who Returns

mentor.speaker: Kyber
mentor.text: Saving somebody today is good. Keeping them alive next week? Annoyingly, that takes more work.

scenes.situation: A recovering patient returns to a field clinic after an earlier injury flares up. The clinic also has several first-time patients needing basic care. You have limited treatment supplies and room, and the returning patient wants a risky quick fix so they can leave immediately.
scenes.question: What do you prioritize?

answers.text: I re-evaluate the returning patient before repeating treatment that may no longer be appropriate.
I design a longer recovery plan and explain why the quick fix may put the patient at greater risk.
I triage the whole clinic and schedule the returning patient without abandoning the new arrivals.
I explore whether the recurring injury has a preventable underlying cause before deciding on treatment.
I prepare a focused additional first-aid intervention if the patient needs it and the rules permit it.

introCandidates.text: Good sabotage doesn't break everything. It breaks the one thing that makes everything else work. Want to cut a circuit, reshape a blast, assemble a turret, or make their whole operation stumble? Let's choose the interesting failure point.

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Saboteur, what kind of disruption or technical expertise do you want to master?

answers.text: I want to use a sudden opening before an enemy has time to defend against it.
I want an unsuspecting guard to suffer the consequences of leaving their defenses open.
I want to interrupt an enemy's decision-making long enough to give the operation time to move.
I want doubt to slow an opponent at the moment they expect to act.
I want to provoke an opponent into mistakes that disrupt their ability to fight.
I want confusion among enemies to upset their coordination without a direct confrontation.
I want repositioning between attacks to make my next shot more dependable.
I want to deny enemies the teamwork bonuses they rely on.
I want intelligence and preparation to turn the enemy's habits against them.
I want a precise attack to weaken the target's next attempt to fight back.
I want a hit against an unprepared enemy to impair their ability to keep fighting.
I want constant movement to improve my attacks without remaining exposed.
I want an opening to take or disable the object an enemy needs for their plan.
I want to interfere with the skill an opponent is depending on to stop us.
I want a surprise opening against an enemy to make a close attack count.
I want to deepen the effectiveness of an ambush when the target is truly vulnerable.
I want social influence to coax information out of someone before they realize the cost.
I want to lock down a computer terminal so that unauthorized operators struggle to gain access.
I want my technical skills to make forged electronic credentials look convincing.
I want to bypass electronic security that would stop an ordinary operator.
I want to follow a transmission or digital trail back to where it began.
I want an electronic device to perform a useful function it was not intended to perform.
I want to introduce software that disrupts the system relying on it.
I want to overcome sophisticated computer defenses through focused technical expertise.
I want to disable a chosen category of nearby electronics without detonating a charge.
I want a blast directed toward its objective instead of spreading equally in every direction.
I want a jammer that interferes with hostile droids while they remain in range.
I want to deploy a mine quickly when the team has little time to prepare.
I want to set a charge faster and with less risk of it detonating during setup.
I want to extend an explosive blast when a larger target truly requires it.
I want a turret to self-destruct when destroyed, denying enemies an intact machine.
I want a sturdier turret I can direct without standing immediately beside it.
I want to construct a temporary automated blaster turret for a specific encounter.
I want a turret designed to incapacitate targets rather than inflict lethal wounds.
I want a tougher deployable turret able to attack twice in a round at an accuracy cost.
I want a turret whose ion attacks disable hostile droids or equipment rather than relying on ordinary damage.
I want enemy weapons to malfunction unexpectedly when a disastrous attack roll exposes their weakness.
I want attacks against unattended equipment and vehicles to be significantly more destructive.
I want to disable increasingly complex equipment with less preparation time.
I want enough technical mastery to retry a failed disable-device or explosives check and keep the better result.
I want to make systems fail in ways that stop the enemy while minimizing harm to people nearby.
Mastering this work is the career I chose. I want to keep learning how things fail, not seek another title.
I have not decided whether I prefer slicing, demolition, turrets, or covert disruption. I want to explore them first.

scenes.title: The Wrong Support Beam

mentor.speaker: Spark
mentor.text: I love a clean failure point. But the wrong one? That is a very expensive lesson.

scenes.situation: A fortified transmission tower is directing hostile drones toward a settlement. The tower stands beside a civilian power substation, and both share an older support platform. A collapse could stop the signal but would likely damage the substation. The mission objective is to interrupt transmissions, not destroy the whole site.
scenes.question: How do you disable the tower?

answers.text: I look for a small, isolated failure point that disables the transmitter without collapsing the support platform.
I use the access controls to shut down the signal rather than placing any explosive charge.
I wait until nearby workers clear the area before attempting to disable the tower.
I set a contingency that disables the signal only if the tower starts directing another drone attack.
I gather more structural information before choosing a method, even if the delay risks losing the opportunity.

scenes.title: The Network That Lies

mentor.speaker: Spark
mentor.text: Systems are honest right up until somebody programs them not to be. That's where the fun starts.

scenes.situation: A logistics network is forwarding location data to an adversary. A legitimate technician account can access a maintenance console, but the network logs also contain emergency medical dispatch records. Disabling the whole system would hide the convoy routes and interrupt aid. The operator requests a targeted solution.
scenes.question: What do you change?

answers.text: I isolate the suspicious forwarding function while keeping the medical dispatch service running.
I examine the transmission records to identify where the information is being sent.
I create a plausible decoy route in the feed so the real convoy can continue unseen.
I preserve an untouched log of the transmissions and report the suspected compromise before modifying the system.
I seek authorization for a narrow, reversible intervention that can be tested without interrupting medical records.

scenes.title: The Temporary Perimeter

mentor.speaker: Spark
mentor.text: Turret problems are wonderful. The important question is what you want the turret to stop.

scenes.situation: A workshop preparing emergency repairs expects hostile droids to approach through two entrances. Engineers must keep moving between rooms, and a fixed automated turret could accidentally block their escape. You have time to plan a defensive emplacement, but no turret is assumed already built.
scenes.question: What defensive plan do you prefer?

answers.text: I plan a turret position where it can cover the hostile approach without firing into the engineers’ escape route.

scenes.title: The Unmarked Patrol

mentor.speaker: Shield Captain Theron
mentor.text: The danger we do not recognize is the one we cannot protect others against.

scenes.situation: You are scouting a ridge ahead of a relief column. Figures in unmarked armor are moving toward the road, but you cannot tell whether they are a hostile patrol or frightened local guards. They have not spotted you, and the column will reach the ridge soon.
scenes.question: What do you do first?

answers.text: I observe their numbers, equipment and behavior long enough to give the column a useful warning.
I follow the patrol’s route from a safe distance to learn where it intends to intercept the road.
I warn the column of an uncertain contact and recommend a temporary halt while I verify the threat.
I find an observation point that keeps me concealed while giving the widest view of both patrol and road.
I look for signs the patrol is avoiding danger itself before treating it as an enemy.

scenes.title: Three Lines of Fire

mentor.speaker: Shield Captain Theron
mentor.text: A single clear sight line can protect more people than a dozen unplanned shots.

scenes.situation: During a reconnaissance exercise, a hostile observation droid watches a narrow pass. One friendly lookout can see its antenna, another its route, and you can see its body through broken cover. The droid will transmit the column’s location if it completes its next scan.
scenes.question: Which method do you use?

answers.text: I identify the droid’s exact position and designate it for the lookout with the clearest follow-up shot.
I take an opening shot meant to weaken its defenses for whoever fires next.
I combine the lookouts’ sight reports into a single firing solution before committing anyone.
I study the exposed antenna and choose the part most likely to disrupt the scan.
I use the cover to wait for a clean shot rather than firing through uncertain concealment.

scenes.title: The Position That Must Hold

mentor.speaker: Shield Captain Theron
mentor.text: Courage does not replace geometry. Choose the cover that gives you time to report.

scenes.situation: A scout observation post is discovered by long-range fire. You can crawl toward a collapsed wall, cross to a drainage ditch, or stay behind a thin service panel to finish transmitting your report. Each position exposes you to a different risk.
scenes.question: How do you respond?

answers.text: I move to solid cover that protects me while leaving a workable line for a final report.
I change position as soon as the enemy starts to aim around the panel.
I keep my head down and endure just long enough to transmit the precise location of the attack.
I watch for a flanking attacker rather than trusting the wall to protect me from every direction.
I reach the drainage ditch before the next area strike, sacrificing visibility for survivability.

scenes.title: The First Shot

mentor.speaker: Shield Captain Theron
mentor.text: The first shot is a responsibility. It tells everyone else what kind of battle follows.

scenes.situation: You find a concealed firing position above a camp where an armed raiding party is preparing to move. They are not yet aware of you. A supply cart nearby may contain stolen medicine, but you cannot tell whether civilians are inside the camp. The relief column needs warning soon.
scenes.question: What is your first action?

answers.text: I observe just long enough to identify the raiders’ route, then send a warning rather than start a fight.
I attack the most dangerous visible weapon from concealment before the group can react.
I choose a shot meant to expose the raiders to the column’s defenders instead of chasing the largest hit.
I stay hidden, reposition and verify whether the supply cart contains people before selecting a target.
I strike an exposed area to disrupt the raiders’ approach, then retreat before they can surround me.

scenes.title: Carry the Warning Home

mentor.speaker: Shield Captain Theron
mentor.text: A warning that dies with its messenger protects no one.

scenes.situation: A storm sweeps across the trail behind your observation post. The direct path back to the column is exposed, a rocky shortcut is difficult to traverse, and a narrow tunnel may be watched by enemy scouts. You have confirmed hostile movement and need to relay it.
scenes.question: How do you get the information back?

answers.text: I take the rocky shortcut and use careful footing to stay ahead of the approaching scouts.
I run the exposed route before the storm closes it, trusting speed rather than concealment.
I shift a fallen obstacle long enough to make a passable route for myself and anyone behind me.
I use cover to approach the tunnel and verify who is watching it before committing to the passage.
I send the shortest reliable warning I can now and then choose the safest route back.

introCandidates.text: The hand that reaches for a weapon has one answer. The empty hand has many. You have earned the right to study beyond the foundations. Will you train your sight, your movement, your hold, or the strike that ends a struggle? Choose with care.

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Martial Arts Master, which discipline of the empty hand do you want to deepen?

answers.text: I want to follow a trail without slowing my pursuit every time the signs become faint.
I want to recognize where an opponent is vulnerable even when their defenses seem difficult to penetrate.
I want to regain the initiative when a fight changes and the next moment becomes decisive.
I want another chance to react before the opponent when our encounter begins.
I want to keep my aim steady when concealment obscures the threat I have spotted.
I want to remain difficult to overwhelm when foes try to trap me between them.
I want my training to protect me when an unseen enemy catches me off guard.
I want to notice the smallest change in my surroundings before it becomes an attack.
I want to refine my unarmed strikes until a small opening can become a decisive blow.
I want each successful strike to disrupt my opponent’s next attack.
I want to use my empty hands to strip an armed opponent of their weapon.
I want an opponent to pay for remaining within my reach when my stance is ready.
I want to control a grapple so my opponent cannot simply pull away from my grip.
I want a well-placed unarmed blow to weaken an opponent’s ability to keep fighting.
I want a successful unarmed strike to interrupt what an opponent can do next.
I want successive unarmed blows to stay accurate rather than lose precision through haste.
I want repeated unarmed attacks to wear down protection that would ordinarily blunt my strikes.
I want an exceptional unarmed hit to create the opening for another immediate strike.
I want to study the foundations of Teräs Käsi until its movements become instinct.
I want to learn the discipline of answering an attack without first reaching for a weapon.
I want to learn how to defend myself through empty-handed control and positioning.
I want to develop unarmed techniques for opponents protected by extraordinary defenses.
I want to deepen the Teräs Käsi tradition beyond its fundamental techniques.
I want my strikes to help me endure the retaliation that follows in a long fight.
I want to defend myself and others without needing a weapon to be close at hand.
I worked to perfect the empty hand. I want to keep refining it without pursuing another title.
I want to explore precision, awareness, grappling, and endurance before choosing the discipline I will perfect.

scenes.title: The Blade in the Market

mentor.speaker: Master Zhen
mentor.text: A weapon can frighten a crowd. The hand that meets it must not become another weapon without thought.

scenes.situation: An armed aggressor threatens a merchant in a crowded market passage. People are close enough that a reckless strike could injure someone else. The aggressor has not noticed the clear path behind you, and you have no weapon in hand.
scenes.question: How do you intervene?

answers.text: I close the distance carefully and try to take the weapon without turning the crowd into the battlefield.
I move between the aggressor and the merchant, keeping my defense intact until the crowd clears.
I use a short, controlled unarmed strike to interrupt the threat instead of trying to overpower them.
I watch their grip and footwork for the moment they can be redirected away from the merchant.
I speak firmly and leave them a route to surrender before I commit to an exchange.

scenes.title: Two Angles, One Breath

mentor.speaker: Master Zhen
mentor.text: One opponent draws the eyes. The other waits for the mind to forget them.

scenes.situation: Two opponents approach from different sides in a training ring. One advances rapidly while the other waits to strike when you turn. The ring is small, and your footing changes on loose sand. The exercise ends if you lose balance or leave the marked boundary.
scenes.question: How do you meet the attack?

answers.text: I keep both opponents in view and change my position so neither reaches my back.
I watch the patient opponent for their first real commitment rather than reacting to every feint.
I move with the first attack, using that momentum to keep the second opponent out of reach.
I meet the first opening with several controlled unarmed attacks while preserving my footing for the second.
I take a defensive stance and let the impatient opponent show me where their balance fails.

scenes.title: The Opponent Who Will Not Fall

mentor.speaker: Master Zhen
mentor.text: Armor is an answer to a certain kind of force. Do not ask that question again and again.

scenes.situation: A physically powerful opponent in reinforced armor blocks a doorway during a rescue. Your hands are empty, and pushing straight through the armor is unlikely to end the struggle quickly. The opponent is aggressive but slow to recover their stance after each charge.
scenes.question: Which technique do you choose?

answers.text: I look for the joint or exposed opening where a precise unarmed blow matters more than brute force.
I build pressure through repeated measured strikes rather than spending everything on one blow.
I redirect the next charge into the doorway frame and use the moment to pass rather than win a contest of strength.
I target the opponent’s balance and make them spend effort recovering before they can attack again.
I keep the exchange short and safe, waiting for an opening to restrain them instead of gambling on damage.

scenes.title: The Grip That Becomes a Trap

mentor.speaker: Master Zhen
mentor.text: A contest of strength ends when someone understands the hold. Not when someone proves they can break a bone.

scenes.situation: A rival challenges you to stop them escaping a practice circle without striking their head or throat. They are stronger than you and know how to shift their weight when grabbed. A successful hold must be controlled; injury would forfeit the exercise.
scenes.question: What approach do you take?

answers.text: I let them commit their weight, then move my grip to the side where their strength cannot help them.
I maintain distance until I can establish one secure hold, rather than reaching repeatedly into a counter.
I use their escape attempt to shift our footing and make their next move harder.
I disengage when the hold becomes unsafe, then take a calmer opening instead of forcing the result.
I finish the exercise by controlling their movement, not by causing injury that violates its purpose.

scenes.title: The Trail and the Last Exchange

mentor.speaker: Master Zhen
mentor.text: Fatigue reveals what the body has memorized. The mind must still decide.

scenes.situation: An opponent carrying stolen medical supplies flees over stony ground, leaving an uneven trail before stopping at a narrow archway. They shift stance and begin attacking in irregular bursts. The trail may reveal another escape route, but fatigue is making both pursuit and defense harder.
scenes.question: How do you use the next exchange?

answers.text: I read the trail and the changes in their footwork before deciding where to close the distance.
I take the smallest opening with one precise strike rather than chase a reckless finishing blow.
I keep my stance and breathing steady so fatigue does not decide my timing for me.
I use one successful hit as the beginning of a controlled second strike, if the opening truly remains.
I step back and reset the distance rather than let the opponent’s new rhythm dictate the rest of the fight.

introCandidates.text: Your oath gives your service its direction; it does not decide every action you will take. An Imperial Knight must guard with judgment, not merely obey with a blade. Will you deepen your defense, your lightsaber discipline, your care for those beside you, or your command of the Force?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Imperial Knight, which duty or discipline will you strengthen first?

answers.text: I want armor to serve me without sacrificing the defensive awareness I have earned through experience.
I want experience and armor to contribute together to my protection instead of competing.
I want to move in armor with the practiced ease of a warrior who understands its limitations.
I want armor to protect me without slowing my movement to those who need me.
I want to use a shield generator more reliably when an enemy presses our position.
I want the protective value of my armor to become a natural part of how I fight.
I want to make a short companion lightsaber an exact part of my dueling technique.
I want years of practice to make my lightsaber strikes more precise.
I want to return an incoming blaster bolt with greater control and economy of movement.
I want a thrown lightsaber to disrupt an enemy who believes distance grants safety.
I want to carry a thrown blade through an engagement and reclaim it through the Force.
I want a successful block to become the moment for a careful counterstrike.
I want every successful lightsaber blow to carry the weight of deeper training.
I want to draw on the Force to survive a strike that would otherwise overwhelm my defenses.
I want the capacity to disable a dangerous foe instead of killing them, while accepting the lasting consequences of that choice.
I want to call upon a practiced lightsaber form again when the situation demands it.
I want to maintain precision when I must deliver several lightsaber attacks.
I want my lightsaber to intercept a melee blow before it reaches me.
I want to turn away blaster fire when distance does not provide protection.
I want a disciplined stance that makes every moment of defense more dependable.
I want my practiced lightsaber hits to be more effective when force is unavoidable.
I want to reach a distant threat with my lightsaber without surrendering the weapon.
I want a blaster bolt I deflect to become a controlled answer to its source.
I want to learn a means of stopping a lightsaber strike when a blade is not available.
I want a redirected blaster bolt to carry greater force once I have turned it away.
I want a lightsaber strike to interfere with an opponent’s ability to move away.
I want to answer a blocked melee blow with a measured immediate attack.
I want a short off-hand lightsaber to remain accurate under pressure.
I want a successful cortosis-gauntlet parry to become an immediate chance to counterattack.
I want the Force to deepen the protection of my armor when a fight turns dangerous.
I want to channel the Force through my armor so it helps me withstand a devastating blow.
I want to integrate my armor and combat experience without giving up sound defensive technique.
I want to meet a hostile lightsaber with a carefully trained cortosis-gauntlet defense.
I want another Knight’s successful strike to fortify my resolve to remain in the fight.
I want to defend an adjacent ally with Block and Deflect, not merely protect myself.
I want a fellow Knight’s effective lightsaber strike to create strength for my own next attack.
I want to master a two-handed lightsaber attack that turns deliberate movement into additional impact.
I want the success of an allied lightsaber wielder to strengthen my defenses as we stand together.
I want to recover spent Force energy after an encounter so I can be ready for the next duty.
I want one carefully chosen Force power to remain dependable even under pressure.
I want disciplined meditation to restore my strength when there is time to recover.
I want to move a small object through the Force quickly when an instant matters.
I want to notice disturbances in the Force without surrendering the initiative.
I want to widen my awareness of the immediate area without losing the moment to act.
I want to make a mental connection more reliably when ordinary communication fails.
I want to serve as a guardian whose loyalty is expressed through restraint and responsible protection.
I set out to earn the responsibilities of an Imperial Knight. I want to perfect this service without chasing another title.
I want to understand whether armor, lightsaber technique, defending allies, or Force discipline should shape my service first.

scenes.title: A Convoy Between Two Fires

mentor.speaker: Dezmin
mentor.text: An oath is tested where another person must trust your restraint.

scenes.situation: A civilian relief convoy is trapped between automated turrets and a collapsed retaining wall. An allied guard has taken position beside the lead transport, and another moves to clear a path. The civilians can remain sheltered only briefly; a direct charge would draw fire toward them.
scenes.question: How do you take responsibility for this passage?

answers.text: I stay close to the guard and focus my blade on intercepting attacks that threaten the people behind us.
I find the turret with the clearest angle and strike precisely enough to give the transports a moment to move.
I watch my ally’s advance and time my own counterattack to support their next opening.
I draw incoming fire away from the crowded transport while we establish more secure cover.
I communicate a deliberate withdrawal sequence rather than ask the civilians to run into an uncertain opening.

scenes.title: The Disarmed Duel

mentor.speaker: Dezmin
mentor.text: Control the exchange. A strike need not become an execution.

scenes.situation: A hostile lightsaber wielder blocks a narrow stairwell to an occupied shelter. Their weapon stance is aggressive, but a gap opens whenever they turn to threaten the people below. You have room for one committed action before the doorway closes.
scenes.question: How do you use the opening?

answers.text: I meet the next strike defensively and counter only when their momentum exposes a clear target.
I aim for the weapon-bearing side to end the threat without making a killing blow my first choice.
I use an off-hand blade only if it offers the shorter, cleaner path through their guard.
I use a measured Force-guided throw to keep them from closing on the civilians.
I maintain precise footing and press with one reliable attack instead of losing control to a long flurry.

scenes.title: The Armor Warning

mentor.speaker: Dezmin
mentor.text: Armor is a tool of service. Do not mistake it for judgment.

scenes.situation: During a hazardous passage, your borrowed armor’s status display reports damage around one joint and a failing shield module. A companion has fallen behind near an exposed doorway. The next corridor has little cover and could bring another close fight.
scenes.question: What receives your attention first?

answers.text: I slow down just enough to stabilize the armor and keep my defenses reliable through the corridor.
I press forward with a controlled pace, trusting movement more than waiting in the exposed passage.
I channel the Force into surviving the next heavy blow long enough to reach the companion.
I ready the gauntlet for the possibility that an armed opponent blocks the doorway.
I use the corridor’s remaining cover to protect both of us rather than count on damaged equipment alone.

scenes.title: Orders and Judgment

mentor.speaker: Dezmin
mentor.text: Duty is not evaded by demanding that another person make the choice.

scenes.situation: Two legitimate authorities request immediate assistance at the same frontier settlement. One asks you to secure the command center; another asks you to keep a medical evacuation corridor open. Neither request contains enough information to know which danger is greater, and the local dispatch network is failing.
scenes.question: How do you approach the competing demands?

answers.text: I check who will be exposed by each delay before agreeing to an order that cannot be reversed.
I prioritize the corridor where people have no other defender and tell the other authority what I can still provide.
I seek a quiet moment to center my judgment rather than decide from fear or anger.
I conserve the resources I may need for the second emergency instead of spending them all on the first.
I state what I do not yet know and ask both parties for a verifiable update before dividing effort.

scenes.title: The Broken Signal

mentor.speaker: Dezmin
mentor.text: A silent channel is not the same thing as an empty battlefield.

scenes.situation: A sensor blackout cuts off the emergency team at a remote relay. One ally is visible across a ravine; others are behind sealed blast doors. The local alarms provide contradictory information, and an unstable mechanical arm is moving above the walkway.
scenes.question: What is the first technique or method you rely on?

answers.text: I test the immediate area for danger rather than follow the loudest false alarm.
I look for a disturbance in the Force that might distinguish a living threat from faulty machinery.
I attempt a brief mental contact with the ally across the ravine instead of shouting over the alarms.
I move the small control lever out of danger if my skill allows it, not the entire broken mechanical arm.
I prepare one Force power that I can execute reliably when the actual threat becomes clear.

introCandidates.text: A living tool does not remain what it was yesterday. Neither does its maker. You have earned the discipline to shape what grows and heals—and what changes another being. Which of those responsibilities will you learn to carry with precision?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Shaper, which part of living technology do you wish to master?

answers.text: I want to use suitable natural materials to provide medical care when a prepared medical kit is unavailable.
I want to administer additional first aid when someone has already received the day’s usual treatment.
I want to perform urgent first aid quickly enough that a crisis does not outpace me.
I want a longer window to attempt to revive someone whose life has just been lost.
I want a failed treatment attempt to avoid making a wounded patient worse.
I want assistants working beside me to contribute more reliably to a difficult treatment.
I want to help a patient draw on their own reserve of strength when the need is immediate.
I want my training to give a difficult medical procedure a better chance of success.
I want to provide a willing patient with temporary resilience through an adrenaline implant, while accounting for its aftermath.
I want a willing ally to gain temporary accuracy through a carefully prepared implant, with its costs understood.
I want to strengthen a willing ally’s damage threshold temporarily through a living implant, without ignoring the recovery required.
I want to enhance a willing ally’s melee impact for one encounter through biotech, while planning for the lasting strain afterward.
I want to give a willing ally temporary speed through an implant, fully aware of the toll it takes after the fight.
I want to stabilize a damaged living device quickly when there is no time for a lengthy repair.
I want a temporary biotech repair to restore more function and last long enough to matter.
I want to improve the care and precision of implant surgery so installing biotech is less dangerous to its recipient.
I want a second chance to repair or modify a living device when my first treatment fails.
I want to alter biotechnology with greater efficiency, reducing wasted time and resources while retaining exact control.
I want deeper understanding of living devices to improve the way I study, modify, and repair them.
I want to understand the tools and obligations of a shaping hand before deciding whether to accept one.
I want my creations to serve a purpose I can defend, rather than shape living things simply because I can.
I intend to perfect the craft of shaping living technology. I need no higher title for that work to matter.
I want to explore repair, medicine, living implants, and new biotech designs before committing to one specialty.

scenes.title: The Living Pump

mentor.speaker: Shaper Urza
mentor.text: A machine that breathes gives you warnings. Learn to listen to them.

scenes.situation: A living irrigation pump pulses irregularly beneath a small settlement. Its nutrient line is blocked, but a hastily cut channel might injure the organism that keeps the settlement supplied with water. There are salvaged tools and a short window before the reservoir runs dry.
scenes.question: How would you address the failure?

answers.text: I examine the living channels and make the smallest repair likely to keep the pump functioning.
I reinforce the damaged tissue temporarily rather than risk a complete rebuild in the field.
I attempt a careful second repair after examining why the first method did not work.
I consider a low-cost redesign that will reduce future failures rather than simply hide this one.
I protect the healthy neighboring tissue before acting on the blocked line.

scenes.title: Triage in a Living Corridor

mentor.speaker: Shaper Urza
mentor.text: The body will not wait for a perfect theory. Neither should the healer.

scenes.situation: After an accident in a bioengineering conservatory, three conscious workers need care. One has a serious wound, one is struggling to remain upright, and the third is stable but cannot be left unattended. Supplies are incomplete. Another worker offers to assist with treatment.
scenes.question: What is your initial priority?

answers.text: I stabilize the most critical wound and spend the first moments on the patient least able to wait.
I assign the assistant a narrow role so their help improves the treatment rather than adding confusion.
I check which patient has already received treatment so another attempt does not exceed safe limits.
I plan for the possibility that an initial treatment fails without making the injury worse.
I prepare for emergency resuscitation if a patient deteriorates beyond ordinary first aid.

scenes.title: The Enhancement Consent

mentor.speaker: Shaper Urza
mentor.text: Improving a living system is easy to describe. The recovery cost is harder to ignore.

scenes.situation: A willing expedition volunteer asks whether a temporary living implant might help them escort a medical carrier through dangerous terrain. The implant options can improve speed, resilience, precision, or strength for a limited encounter, but the ensuing physical penalty is severe and persistent until treated or rested away.
scenes.question: What guides your recommendation?

answers.text: I discuss the speed option while making clear that the recovery period could make the return journey harder.
I weigh temporary resilience against the danger of worsening the volunteer’s condition afterward.
I offer the precision option only if the mission truly needs an increased chance of accurate action.
I compare the strength and adrenaline options and help the volunteer choose based on their specific assignment.
I refuse to proceed until the volunteer understands the cost and the procedure is actually safe to attempt.

scenes.title: The Unfinished Design

mentor.speaker: Shaper Urza
mentor.text: A design can be clever and still unworthy of deployment.

scenes.situation: A research enclosure contains a new living sensor that reacts beautifully to movement—but repeatedly harms the small organisms it uses to calibrate itself. A supervisor wants a quick demonstration. A second researcher has proposed an alternative that may take much longer to evaluate.
scenes.question: How would you approach the choice?

answers.text: I document the harm precisely and require safer tests before any public demonstration.
I propose a reversible adjustment to the sensor rather than replacing living components without understanding them.
I ask who will bear the consequences if the sensor is deployed before its behavior is understood.
I study the traditions governing shaping hands and decide whether their obligations match the work I want to do.
I compare alternative prototypes and record the limits of what our tests actually demonstrate.

scenes.title: The Last Procedure

mentor.speaker: Shaper Urza
mentor.text: When two systems are failing, understanding which one is alive is not enough.

scenes.situation: A small mobile clinic relies on a bioengineered filtration unit. A patient needs another procedure, while the filter’s living membrane begins to fail. Only one workstation has power, and moving either the patient or the filter would create additional risk.
scenes.question: What comes first in your plan?

answers.text: I repeat the relevant diagnosis carefully before attempting treatment that might worsen the patient’s condition.
I help the conscious patient use their own limited reserve while we prepare a safer procedure.
I arrange a temporary repair to the filter so the clinic can retain a safe treatment area.
I explain both risks openly and seek a decision from those whose lives will be affected.
I accept that a capable Shaper must sometimes choose which work to defer, without claiming certainty I do not have.

introCandidates.text: Heard you qualified to make a name disappear. Cute. The hard part isn’t landing a shot—it’s knowing when to move, when to wait, and how to get out. So what’s your specialty gonna be?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Assassin, what technique or discipline do you want to develop?

answers.text: I want to exploit the instant a fight begins, before my target has settled into a defense.
I want to make an unexpected hit count when an opponent cannot properly guard against it.
I want misdirection to throw a target off balance before anyone commits to the next move.
I want a moment of uncertainty to steal the action an opponent needed to stop me.
I want to control nearby space so a careless enemy has to reckon with my position.
I want to turn a target’s uncertainty into confusion that affects the people around them.
I want to remain dangerous while moving, not only while holding a perfect firing position.
I want to interfere with an enemy’s plans without having to overpower them directly.
I want a well-timed decision to make my allies more effective when our approach changes.
I want a precise hit to leave a target less capable of continuing the fight.
I want a strike against an exposed target to leave them worse off than the wound alone would suggest.
I want constant movement to create a stronger advantage in the attacks that follow.
I want to take something important away from an enemy while exploiting a close opening.
I want to interrupt the technique or advantage an opponent expects to rely on.
I want my positioning with allies to turn a distracted opponent into a vulnerable one.
I want my attacks against unguarded enemies to become more decisive as my skill grows.
I want charm and apparent harmlessness to create openings that brute force cannot.
I want a carefully applied poison to leave a victim unable to defend as effectively while it takes hold.
I want to adapt the delivery of a poison when circumstances make the usual method impossible.
I want to master the precise application of toxins to a suitable blade rather than depend on a crude strike.
I want my poisons to be harder for a victim’s body to resist.
I want the effects of a poison I have used to be harder to treat or neutralize.
I want my attacks against a target I have marked to grow more dangerous through practiced precision.
I want to settle my aim quickly when a target enters close firing distance.
I want to strike at close range and withdraw before an enemy can pin me down.
I want an accurately prepared shot to overcome defenses that protect targets farther away.
I want to carry the lessons of my first marked-target discipline into a more demanding level of mastery.
I want a close-range precision shot to inflict damage beyond what an ordinary hit could do.
I want the defeat of one foe to give me a chance to act again before the battlefield settles.
I want to change position by a small, deliberate step without handing an enemy an easy opening.
I want to exploit opponents who are already outmaneuvered, rather than force every advantage alone.
I want the defeat of a chosen target to unsettle the other enemies who witness it.
I want to use the pressure of an attack to steer an opponent into a mistake that benefits me.
I want to refine that manipulation until a successful strike creates a more consequential opening.
I want influence over the outcome of a conflict without making my own role obvious.
I want to study a chosen opponent closely enough that each encounter with them becomes more dangerous for them.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to be exact about when force is necessary instead of making violence my answer to every problem.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I worked to become an Assassin. I could spend the rest of my career perfecting this trade without pursuing another title.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to understand the differences between stealth, sniping, maneuver, poisons, and manipulation before choosing my specialty.
