scenes.title: A Rooftop with Two Exits

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Nice angle. Terrible assumptions. Fix the second part.

scenes.situation: You are watching a dangerous courier from the upper level of a crowded transit station. Their route crosses a public walkway and then splits between two guarded exits. Your objective is to stop the courier carrying an encrypted case, but you do not yet know which exit they will choose or whether their guards are aware of you.
scenes.question: What is your first move?

answers.text: I study both exits and hold position until I can isolate the courier without involving the crowd.
I look for a brief, clear shot at the case or its carrier only after I know what the line of fire contains.
I reposition to a second angle where the guards cannot see me approach the closer exit.
I try to identify which guard actually controls the exits so I can disrupt the right person.
I wait for the courier to pass the public walkway before committing to an interception.

scenes.title: The Uncertain Vial

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: A vial nobody checked? Great. That’s how a clean operation turns into a funeral.

scenes.situation: At a remote security post, an armed opponent carries a sealed toxin vial alongside their usual equipment. A nearby technician is already ill, and an unlabelled antidote kit is locked inside the post. You need the suspect stopped and the technician protected, but guessing what the vial contains could make matters worse.
scenes.question: What do you do first?

answers.text: I identify the dangerous material and keep it from being released before I consider any other attack.
I try to disarm the opponent or force them away from the technician before a vial can be used.
I study the material and its delivery limits so I do not make the danger worse through a careless choice.
I make the technician’s evacuation the priority and leave the vial untouched until it can be assessed.
I avoid using the suspect’s own toxin against them until its effect and consequences can be established.

scenes.title: The Message Behind the Contract

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Somebody wants you to pull one string so you don’t notice the other four.

scenes.situation: A mysterious client sends a packet identifying a supposed traitor in a local supply network. A second message arrives anonymously, warning that the client altered the original evidence. Two intermediaries are waiting for instructions, and neither knows what the other has been told.
scenes.question: How do you determine your response?

answers.text: I compare the two messages and trace where the claims conflict before acting against anyone.
I ask each intermediary separate, narrow questions to learn who is trying to influence the other.
I reveal only a small harmless detail to see whether it reaches the person manipulating the messages.
I prepare a way to disrupt the instigator’s next move instead of attacking the named suspect immediately.
I make the consequences of a hostile attack visible enough to deter the other intermediaries from escalating.

scenes.title: The Exit After the Strike

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Everybody plans the entry. That’s why the exit’s where the amateurs get caught.

scenes.situation: An attempted interception has forced the courier to abandon the encrypted case. The corridor shutters start closing, guards are approaching from two directions, and the only route to a public transport platform crosses an exposed loading gantry. You can retreat, interfere with the guards, or try to secure the case.
scenes.question: Which method would you use?

answers.text: I move through the nearest unguarded gap before it closes, even if it means leaving the case behind.
I use the guards’ poor alignment to cross where they cannot support each other.
I interrupt the guard carrying the shutter control so the escape route stays open longer.
I keep up a moving defense that discourages pursuit while I guide the others out.
I recover the case only if it can be taken without trapping the entire group on the gantry.

scenes.title: The Wrong Target

mentor.speaker: Delta
mentor.text: Bad intel gets people hurt. Worse intel makes you think the job’s done.

scenes.situation: At the last moment before a planned confrontation, the person you expected to intercept is replaced by someone wearing the same uniform. An ally believes the replacement is the real target, while a frightened witness insists they have seen two identical uniforms moving in opposite directions.
scenes.question: What do you do now?

answers.text: I delay the confrontation until I can confirm which person actually matches the evidence.
I reposition quietly so I can observe both routes without alerting either uniformed person.
I create a harmless distraction to test which person reacts to the hidden signal.
I warn my ally that certainty is missing and arrange a fallback rather than let them act alone.
I accept that abandoning this attempt may be better than acting against the wrong person.

introCandidates.text: Darling, a convincing smile opens more doors than a blaster ever will. After that, it’s a question of timing: a well-placed lie, a useful distraction, or a little luck. Which part of the art would you like to perfect?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Charlatan, what kind of social craft or calculated misdirection do you want to master?

answers.text: I want people studying my manner and intentions to come away with less certainty, not more.
I want an artful feint to make an opponent vulnerable to the allies fighting beside me.
I want to talk a hostile person into withholding an attack, even if only for a moment.
I want a few carefully chosen words before a fight to help my allies move into better positions.
I want a sharp rebuke to unsettle an opponent before their next decision.
I want to use conflicting appearances and sudden betrayals to control how an opponent reacts.
I want enemies to underestimate me as harmless until their next attack is already compromised.
I want to position myself beside another person and make that proximity protect me from an attack.
I want a successful feint to create room for me to move before the opponent adjusts.
I want to talk a target into revealing an opening that my allies can exploit.
I want a perfectly timed warning or distraction to help an ally evade an incoming attack.
I want my apparent cooperation to conceal the moment when I turn the situation to my advantage.
I want one streak of outrageous luck to carry me through a task I had no business attempting.
I want an unlikely angle or bouncing shot to reach an opponent who thought they were safe.
I want one fortunate opening to salvage a shot that would normally miss.
I want a bad decision to leave me one last lucky chance rather than a certain failure.
I want to read a wager well enough to risk my credits only when the odds can turn my way.
I want a stroke of fortune to prevent the hit that would otherwise bring me down.
I want a particularly successful move to grant me the momentum to do something more.
I want a second attempt when I fumble a skill I normally know well.
I want to survive the unexpected blow that should have ended my story.
I want an improbable attack to work when my ordinary methods have run out.
I want my thoughts to be difficult to predict or manipulate when someone probes for a weakness.
I want to turn an extraordinary stroke of luck into a way around a dangerous situation.
I want one last chance to prevent a catastrophe just as it is about to happen.
I want to turn my practiced charm into real opportunities for credits and favors.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to become better at winning a valuable concession from someone convinced the deal was their idea.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to solve problems through negotiation, appearances, and nerve rather than force.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I chose the art of the con as my career. I do not need another title to keep getting better at it.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to explore deception, luck, influence, and distraction before deciding what kind of Charlatan I will be.

scenes.title: The Wrong Guest List

mentor.speaker: Silvertongue Sela
mentor.text: Oh, a guest list. A tiny document with such an inflated opinion of itself.

scenes.situation: A reception controls access to a hearing where a witness intends to speak. A guard discovers that your name appears on the wrong list, and two guests have begun arguing loudly over who has permission to enter. You may have only a short conversation before the doors close.
scenes.question: How do you handle the social pressure?

answers.text: I give a calm, plausible explanation and let the guard correct the list without feeling challenged.
I redirect the argument between guests so their own words clarify which door is actually open.
I feign confusion long enough to slip into the correct line while attention moves elsewhere.
I enlist an ally to answer the guard while I identify what the guest list actually controls.
I choose one claim I can support instead of weaving a story too elaborate to survive another question.

scenes.title: A Familiar Face in the Crowd

mentor.speaker: Silvertongue Sela
mentor.text: If they think you’re harmless, darling, consider it a compliment you can spend later.

scenes.situation: A courier carrying testimony notices someone following them across a packed market. You are nearby, but the pursuer does not know you are involved. The courier may panic if approached too directly, and a sudden fight would endanger shoppers.
scenes.question: What kind of intervention do you make?

answers.text: I approach as an ordinary shopper and offer a believable reason for the courier to leave with me.
I use the busy crowd to shield our movement without dragging shoppers into a direct fight.
I call out a perfectly timed warning so the courier sees the dangerous turn before taking it.
I keep my true purpose difficult to read and test whether the follower is reacting to me or the courier.
I change the courier’s expectations with an honest warning rather than build another lie that could collapse.

scenes.title: The Debt Behind the Favor

mentor.speaker: Silvertongue Sela
mentor.text: That sounds like a favor. Check the price tag before you smile.

scenes.situation: A shipping broker agrees to release emergency cargo only after someone settles an old disputed invoice. The broker would prefer credits, but a union representative argues the delay violates an earlier promise. Each party has a different account of the original agreement.
scenes.question: How would you seek an outcome?

answers.text: I compare the two accounts and try to offer a deal that gives both parties something they can verify.
I ask the broker which single concession would matter most instead of haggling blindly.
I attempt the difficult calculation myself and use an improved second try if I genuinely have the training for it.
I risk a small, clearly bounded wager to break the stalemate without putting the cargo itself at stake.
I prioritize preventing the cargo from being lost while the parties keep disputing who owes what.

scenes.title: Odds That Changed at Midnight

mentor.speaker: Silvertongue Sela
mentor.text: The odds moved. Sweetheart, that’s not bad news; that’s news.

scenes.situation: At a crowded game hall, the winnings from a legitimate contest could pay for urgent passage offworld. A rival announces they have changed the final terms; another guest offers a side bet that would cover the cost but adds considerable risk. Security is watching for disturbances.
scenes.question: How would you play the next moment?

answers.text: I check the actual rules and change my approach rather than betting on the rival’s confidence.
I accept only the smaller wager that I can afford to lose if the other offer is a trap.
I exploit one unexpected opening in the rules without trying to change the whole contest.
I keep an exit and backup plan in mind in case the room becomes hostile instead of debating the wager.
I use the rival’s attempt to impress the room as a chance to redirect attention toward a fair outcome.

scenes.title: The Story That Almost Worked

mentor.speaker: Silvertongue Sela
mentor.text: And there it is—the moment a beautiful story meets an inconvenient fact.

scenes.situation: You propose a compromise to two rival merchants. One quietly produces records that contradict an assumption behind your argument. The merchants are listening, but their patience is nearly gone; neither is committed to violence or deceit yet.
scenes.question: What do you do after being challenged?

answers.text: I correct the assumption and build a smaller agreement around the facts we can still verify.
I turn the question back to what each merchant actually needs and let them argue less about my wording.
I make a light joke to buy one moment to examine the newly revealed record.
I withdraw the disputed claim rather than demand that everyone believe an account I can no longer support.
I ask for a pause because I still cannot tell which strategy will produce a workable agreement.

introCandidates.text: Okay, so you’ve got no tools, half a broken machine, and exactly the wrong spare parts. That’s practically a vacation! Are we fixing something, making something, or finding the one person who has what we need?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As an Improviser, what problem-solving specialty do you want to develop?

answers.text: I want to tune a powered weapon for the encounter at hand without rebuilding it from scratch.
I want a hurried field repair to keep failing machinery useful long enough to matter.
I want my mechanical knowledge to help me bypass computerized access when a console stands in the way.
I want to patch equipment before it completely fails, buying the team a little more time.
I want to find the right replacement parts and help others restore more from a difficult repair.
I want the equipment I obtain for the team to be tougher and easier to maintain.
I want to source expertly modified gear without paying an extra premium for every improvement.
I want to locate someone who can supply restricted equipment without wasting days searching.
I want to produce the tool that lets an ally attempt a specialized task they were not trained to handle.
I want to bring a badly damaged machine back into the fight with one fast, reliable repair.
I want to turn spare parts into a temporary but functional device when proper equipment is unavailable.
I want to reactivate a disabled enemy droid and temporarily bring it to our side.
I want to apply a specialist modification to a device I assemble in the field.
I want an improvised explosive to deliver more force when a carefully measured blast is required.
I want to work with incomplete equipment and still find a workable technical solution.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to maintain access to useful hard-to-find gear when ordinary supplies cannot meet the mission.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want people to know that a broken plan is still solvable when I am around.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I wanted a career making things work. I can keep refining that craft without chasing another class.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to try repairs, custom gear, sourcing supplies, and field inventions before deciding where to specialize.

scenes.title: The Jammed Hatch

mentor.speaker: Lucky Jack
mentor.text: Door’s stuck. Tool kit’s gone. Fantastic—we’re down to the fun options.

scenes.situation: An emergency hatch refuses to open as smoke creeps down a corridor. The access panel is damaged, the nearest toolbox has been emptied, and a service drone is still using the adjacent repair junction. The group needs a safe route but could lose valuable time trying to force the door.
scenes.question: What do you work on first?

answers.text: I use the damaged junction as the starting point for a fast mechanical repair, even without a complete kit.
I patch the hatch’s simplest failed component before committing to a full rebuild.
I borrow a usable part from the service drone only after checking whether that would disable a second essential system.
I test whether I can reach the lock from a different service interface instead of cutting the door open.
I give the group a firm time to attempt repair, then switch to a safer route if the hatch stays jammed.

scenes.title: The Workbench of Spare Parts

mentor.speaker: Lucky Jack
mentor.text: A beautiful machine? We don’t have time for beautiful. We have time for useful.

scenes.situation: A transport must cross a damaged loading bridge. Its guidance beacon is broken, and you have assorted parts, a small power cell and a working blaster. You can rebuild the beacon, fashion a temporary locator, or tune another device for the crossing. The bridge will become impassable if repairs take too long.
scenes.question: What do you make or adjust?

answers.text: I assemble a temporary locator from spare components and accept that it may be useful only for this crossing.
I modify a working instrument rather than gamble on a completely new prototype.
I find which substitute parts match the beacon and use only those, keeping the rest available for later failures.
I check the powered weapon for a repairable component that could safely provide a useful temporary output.
I reduce the crossing to one simple test and stop revising the design once the test is good enough.

scenes.title: The Supplier’s Locked Counter

mentor.speaker: Lucky Jack
mentor.text: Well, now we’re shopping. Somebody hide the credit account from me.

scenes.situation: A medical relay station needs replacement tools and protective equipment before an approaching storm. Local sellers have an incomplete catalog, and one specialist claims the best components are restricted stock. Several cheaper alternatives are available but may fail during the repair.
scenes.question: How would you obtain what is needed?

answers.text: I compare durability and repair needs before selecting the least fragile available kit.
I look for a specialist supplier who already has suitably modified gear rather than pay to rebuild it ourselves.
I explore legal alternatives first, then investigate restricted supply channels only if the task genuinely demands them.
I identify which one tool would let an ally carry out the repair instead of buying everything on the list.
I reserve scarce components for the critical repair and postpone the upgrades that can wait until later.

scenes.title: The Shutdown Droid

mentor.speaker: Lucky Jack
mentor.text: Okay, that droid’s down. We could fix it, borrow its brain, or, hear me out, not make things worse.

scenes.situation: A security droid has been disabled in a depot that is losing power. It could potentially be reactivated to reach a sealed control station, but another injured service droid is nearby. A timed failsafe is about to seal the depot’s exits.
scenes.question: Which intervention do you choose?

answers.text: I try the control station’s own access panel first rather than rely on controlling the disabled droid.
I consider activating the disabled security droid only after accounting for its limited and destructive aftermath.
I attempt a bounded temporary repair on the injured service droid to restore a safer alternative.
I prepare a controlled diversion only if the doors cannot be opened through repair or access controls.
I split attention between the droid and the timer, stopping any experiment that risks trapping us inside.

scenes.title: A Plan That Outlived Its Parts

mentor.speaker: Lucky Jack
mentor.text: First idea broke? Excellent. Now we know exactly one thing that doesn’t work.

scenes.situation: A team attempts to set up a temporary field transmitter from salvaged equipment. The signal reaches its destination but fails unpredictably when the equipment overheats. You have enough material for one more adjustment before the receiver window closes, and nobody agrees on the source of the fault.
scenes.question: How do you make the next decision?

answers.text: I run the smallest test that distinguishes a heat problem from a power problem before changing anything else.
I make a reversible alteration and keep the old parts ready in case the output degrades.
I ask each teammate for the part of the failure they actually observed instead of voting on guesses.
I choose the reliable but less ambitious signal if it will reach the receiver before the window closes.
I leave the specialization open until I know which kind of technical challenge keeps recurring in my work.

introCandidates.text: Finding a route is the easy part. Making sure everyone can use it—and has somewhere defensible to stop—is the job. So what are you developing: sharper reconnaissance, better movement, or positions the whole team can trust?

questionCandidates.label: Q1
questionCandidates.text: As a Pathfinder, what part of scouting and establishing safe ground do you want to master?

answers.text: I want to follow difficult trails so our group is not led astray by fading evidence.
I want to identify a flaw in an enemy’s protection when ordinary attacks cannot get through.
I want to recover the advantage of timing after a fight begins to turn against us.
I want to recognize the start of trouble before the rest of the group is caught flat-footed.
I want to remain accurate when smoke, poor light, or concealment obscures a threat.
I want to remain aware enough that enemies on opposite sides cannot easily trap me.
I want a sudden ambush to find me ready to defend myself.
I want to notice small changes in terrain or sound before they endanger the team.
I want to get clear of the worst of explosions and other broad attacks.
I want a brief burst of strength when a barrier blocks the only safe route.
I want to cross dangerous ground quickly when the others need a route opened.
I want to move across rough terrain without losing ground to it.
I want enemies firing into our prepared position to have a harder time landing their shots.
I want to move with a nearby ally so neither of us is stranded while changing position.
I want to help someone make more effective use of the cover they already have.
I want to identify a defensible area where my allies can withstand danger more confidently.
I want the ground around our safe position to slow enemies trying to rush us.
I want to abandon an old position deliberately and help my team move swiftly toward the next one.
I want allies advancing out of our secure position to strike with better timing.
I want injured allies who catch their breath inside our secure position to recover more strength.
I want to find a firing angle from cover without wasting time lining up a distant target.
I want to give an ally a clear moment to move and be ready to punish anyone who attacks them in transit.
I want to turn nearby terrain and loose materials into useful cover before the enemy closes in.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want the people following my route to reach their destination alive, not merely arrive first.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I worked to find ground worth defending and help others hold it. I could do this for my entire career.

sourceRef.heading: Class features, personal identity, capstone and neutral

answers.text: I want to develop my eye for terrain, my survival skills, and my ability to prepare safe positions before choosing a specialty.

scenes.title: The Washed Crossing

mentor.speaker: Lead
mentor.text: That crossing looked fine yesterday. Terrain doesn’t owe us consistency.

scenes.situation: A sudden storm has washed out the bridge to a remote village. The river is rising, the slopes above it are unstable, and a small group of travelers needs a route before dark. A faint track leads toward the ridge, but it may be a dead end.
scenes.question: What do you check or choose first?

answers.text: I examine the faint ridge track and test whether it remains usable beyond the first bend.
I identify the most stable high ground before committing the group to any route.
I establish a temporary defensible waiting area so travelers are not exposed while we test the crossing.
I watch for signs of movement or ambush above the ridge while another traveler checks the river.
I identify a fallback route first, even if the primary path appears passable.

scenes.title: Cover That Will Not Last

mentor.speaker: Lead
mentor.text: That wall stops sight, maybe. It won’t stop everything. Measure your assumptions.

scenes.situation: A medical team must wait beside an exposed communications shelter for a shuttle pickup. Low crates, broken masonry and scattered machine housings offer partial protection. A hostile patrol may arrive before the shuttle, and the surrounding ground is too open for an easy escape.
scenes.question: How do you make the position safer?

answers.text: I choose the part of the shelter with the strongest existing cover and adjust how the team uses it.
I prepare an approach that slows a patrol reaching the shelter without trapping our own evacuees.
I lay out a protected area where wounded travelers can recover while the pickup is delayed.
I identify one firing position that provides cover without losing sight of the likely approach.
I use loose material to build extra cover only if the time and tools make it practical.

scenes.title: The Relocation Window

mentor.speaker: Lead
mentor.text: Holding is easy to say. Moving without becoming targets is the useful skill.

scenes.situation: A scouting party has made a temporary safe position in a rocky hollow. A friendly messenger arrives with news that the intended destination has moved. The group must cross open ground to a second hollow while hostile observers may be tracking the route.
scenes.question: How do you arrange the movement?

answers.text: I coordinate with a nearby ally so we move together rather than leave one person isolated on the crossing.
I select a new protected position and call the relocation only when the route is clear enough to risk.
I ready a supporting action at the launch point so others can move at the right moment.
I cover an ally’s move and remain ready to answer anyone who attacks them during the crossing.
I cross the most exposed stretch quickly and then scout back for whoever is still moving.

scenes.title: A Signal in the Dust

mentor.speaker: Lead
mentor.text: One footprint’s wrong. That’s usually the one that matters.

scenes.situation: A forward team receives a garbled warning as dust blows across an old trade road. Two sentries appear at opposite ends of a shallow canyon, and a flare ignites near the group’s intended exit. You have only a moment to assess whether the team is being drawn into an ambush.
scenes.question: How do you respond to the warning?

answers.text: I identify the probable ambush line and warn the group before anyone charges toward the flare.
I keep moving defensively in case the sentries are trying to trap us between their positions.
I brace for an area attack and take the best available escape route rather than trying to outshoot the flare.
I adjust our order of movement as the situation changes so we can regain initiative after the first shock.
I try to distinguish the actual threat from dust and misdirection before choosing the direction of retreat.

scenes.title: The Route Nobody Likes

mentor.speaker: Lead
mentor.text: Every route costs something. Pick the cost you can actually pay.

scenes.situation: A group must deliver life-support filters across uneven ground before a shelter’s reserves run low. One route climbs a steep ridge and risks exhaustion; another is longer but offers stable footing; a third passes through a narrow defile with a damaged gate. The travelers are tired, and weather is changing.
scenes.question: Which responsibility do you take first?

answers.text: I test the damaged gate and use a brief burst of strength only if it can safely open the defile.
I select the longer stable route if it gives every traveler a realistic chance to arrive safely.
I scout the ridge alone only far enough to verify the first obstacle before asking anyone else to climb.
I organize short rest and carry rotations so exhaustion does not decide the outcome for the weakest traveler.
I explain the tradeoffs plainly and choose a route we can revise if the terrain proves worse than expected.
